subtopic: REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS AND MOUNTED POLICE
REQUEST FOR INCREASE IN PENSIONS OF SUPERANNUATED CIVIL SERVANTS AND MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were retired, after long service, when salaries were low, so as to bring their pensions in line with those of the present.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity of moving this resolution, because I do not think there is a hardship in Canada today that would compare with what the retired civil servants of this country are suffering. I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not in his seat. I see the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) is here, and I expect to hear him step on it and just go because he is convinced, as I am, that this resolution is right.
I am not going to spend any time quoting the outstanding speeches which were made last year by the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the Minister of Public Works and the Minister of Finance, or the outstanding speech which was made by the former leader of the opposition. To me this resolution indicates an outstanding need. I have come to the place where I do not care very much which party grants this increase in pension to our former civil servants. Whether it is the Liberal party, the Conservative party or the party which is not as good as either, it does not matter very much so long as we get this increase. I have been at this for a number of years but that does not matter now. We are at it now and we mean what we say.
There are two reasons why I bring forth this resolution. The first is the justice of it, and the second, the need for it. Every member of this house will realize, Mr. Speaker, that there is one petition in the prayer given by our Divine Leader, namely that the government may have truth and justice, religion and piety. I am emphasizing truth and justice now, and my first argument is justice. This increase in pensions is absolutely just. Therefore if it is not granted the government will be doing an injustice to the retired civil servants.
I should like to quote just a little bit of the speech of the Minister of Public Works: "The clear understanding was that the basis of this superannuation itself when it was first introduced was that they receive a stated percentage of their pay when they retired which would be sufficient for them to maintain approximately the same standard of living they had received before they retired." The

law of this country is a guarantee to the civil servant when he enters the service that when he retires he will have a pension that will help him maintain the standard of living he had before. If the government does not do that, then it is not practising truth and justice.
Another reason it is just is that these people themselves contributed to their pensions during all the years they were working, and they are not getting a square deal. Many of them worked ten hours a day six days a week. Those doing the same jobs now only work eight hours a day and five days a week. Therefore I say that if retired civil servants do not get a pension in proportion to the salaries being paid now they are not being treated justly.
Other countries like New Zealand, Australia and Great Britain have increased civil service pensions. Great Britain has made six increases. The United States has kept up to date but poor Canada cannot afford to pay retired civil servants the pensions they were promised by law. I read the local Ottawa newspapers fairly regularly. In the Ottawa Citizen of December 12 there was an article by J. A. Hume with the heading, "Civil Service Superannuation Fund Up." In that article he stated:
At the end of the last fiscal year on March 31, the public service superannuation fund had a balance of $918,943,986 to its credit on the government's books. This represented an increase of $114,707,703 on the year's operations.
Therefore I say that if the government keeps piling up the superannuation fund and does not pay the pensions it promised by law it is not acting justly. If anybody can suggest stronger language to use I will be very glad to use it. I say the government is not acting justly toward retired civil servants in not granting an increase in their superannuation.
There is a need. I and other hon. members have received a submission by the civil service association of Ottawa in which some cases of need are outlined. The association tells us about a man who had to give up his apartment because his rent went up from $30 a month to $83. Another person had to leave his apartment, and others have had to cut down on clothes and recreation.
But the association did not give all the outstanding needs. I know a man in Fort William who, as I stated last year, had to give up his pipe. When a man has smoked for 40 or 50 years and has to give up his pipe so his wife can have a few more of the luxuries of life he is being hard hit, and it is not fair. If some of you had to give up your pipes you would be rooting around like wild
Public Service-Pensions men. I know when our hired man did not have his pipe we were advised to keep out of the way of his big boots, because he was not normal. When a man has to give up his pipe because the government does not pay him the pension he should have I say the government is not acting justly. I think that is strong enough language.
Some people say this country is hard up. I have listened to the members of the C.C.F. and Social Credit groups, who tell us how hard up the farmers are. I tell you their condition would not compare with that of the retired civil servants. If one compared the three meals a day which the farmers have with the two meals a day which our retired civil servants often have, then one would change his mind and be glad he was a farmer. I should like to prove the fact that this country is not hard up. I have here a report from the dominion bureau of statistics which proves that the people of this country spend $512 million on tobacco and $965 million on liquor. This means that a total of $1,477 million goes up in smoke or down the drain. If these luxuries were taxed in a small way the revenue would pay for larger pensions of our retired civil servants.
I am not going to say very much more, because I intend to keep my reputation for not making long speeches. I do not think it is necessary to do so. As the Minister of Public Works said last year, a speech on this question is not necessary. I am just stating that because of these two things, the outstanding need of the civil servants and because of the law of the land, the government should grant an increase in these pensions. As I look at my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works and think of the speeches he has made in the past 22 years and the cooperation he has given in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I often feel he meant what he said. If he meant what he said we will have this increase in pensions. I cannot do better in closing than to quote the recommendations of this civil service association. They are as follows:
(1)	That the government increase the pensions of all those now on superannuation by restoring the full purchasing power of the original pension: and
(2)	That the government safeguard the future purchasing power of pensions by granting an increase in pension payments corresponding to the percentage of any general salary increase;
(3)	That the costs of the increases recommended be borne solely by the superannuation fund of the public service of Canada, without any increase in contribution rates.
Mr. Speaker, my last words are these. After I get my cheque and before I hand it over to somebody who knows more about spending it than I do, if somebody were to say to me "Hands up", and I handed over my salary

Public Service-Pensions you would call that highway robbery. But when the government say by law that you are going to get a pension according to your standard of living and then they fall down on it, what would you call that? I will not call it highway robbery, but if I were to use the language of the hon. member for Vancouver East I would use another word which I will not use here.
I appreciate your courtesy, Mr. Speaker, in listening to me for these 19 minutes.

In the legislation there is also a ceiling of $4,104, or in other words the increases will not apply to increase a pension beyond that amount. In congress there appears to have been little concern over what the public may have thought about these special provisions for retired civil servants, but perhaps this could be accounted for by the fact that it is now the accepted practice in that country to increase the benefits of recipients under their old age and survivors' insurance scheme after retirement without, of course, requiring any additional contribution. In this parliament I can find only one precedent for this type of action which is suggested, that being an amendment to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act in 1925 to provide an increase in pensions granted prior to July 7, 1919 so as to bring them up
to the same pension level as if the pensioners were retiring on the effective date of the amendment but with the service which was to their credit at the date of actual retirement. There was a further amendment to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act in 1930 which resulted in a readjustment of pensions, but by a means not material to this discussion.
In the provinces so far as I have been able to ascertain there is no general pattern. Three provinces, British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Newfoundland have some provision. The province of British Columbia pays $1 per month for each year of service from the date of retirement until age 70, when this additional payment stops on the ground that the pensioner then receives old age security. In the province of Saskatchewan, under an order in council a bonus is payable to retired civil servants between ages 65 and 70. The bonus is a maximum of $45 additional per month provided it does not bring the combined pension and bonus above $75. The bonus ceases at age 70 when old age security payments commence. Thus it would seem to me that the position taken in British Columbia and Saskatchewan and the technique employed there relates wholly to the so-called

Public Service-Pensions hardship cases and not to the general problem we are considering in the house today.
I have not been able to ascertain in detail the situation in Newfoundland. Apparently it is under an order in council, because I have not been able to find any legislative authority. The other provinces appear to have made no provision, although it should be said that in most provinces the pension is based on an average of the last three years of salary and therefore the pension bears a closer relationship to the retiring salary.

speechtext:
Yes, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is quite correct. In the province of Ontario provision has been made in respect of retired teachers, although that provision has not been applied to retired civil servants generally as yet. With regard to private Canadian employers there are isolated instances of pension increases to former employees but no general pattern appears to have developed yet.
I have taken the time of the house to make this rather comprehensive review of the legislation and the practice in other jurisdictions in order to show two things.
First, there is no insuperable obstacle to a just and fair readjustment of civil service pensions. On the contrary, it is possible, it is feasible and it is just, and it has been so established elsewhere. Secondly, the techniques of adjustment, or perhaps I should say of readjustment, are not simple; and to establish a relative justice between all classes of retired civil servants requires the most detailed investigation and study which are now proceeding with the greatest possible rapidity.
I confess, sir, that when I first started to study this problem I believed that if the government were disposed to act, the best and the simplest solution would be an overall percentage increase. And I think, from my review of the debates in this house, that that has been the more usual approach to the problem. But I have reached the conclusion, I have to say, that such an approach would create more injustices than it could possibly cure. In this respect there is a most apt reference on a slightly different point by Mr. Henry Brooke, to whom I have already referred, the financial secretary to the treasury, in introducing the United Kingdom
[Mr. Bell (Carleton) .1
bill on February 23, 1956, and I quote from page 588 of the British Hansard of that day:
Most unfortunately, the more one studies that seemingly attractive possibility, the more convinced one becomes that it would be impossible that way to do individual justice.
What we have to do is to take into account a total body of about 600,000 pensioners, who have retired after different kinds of services, with different kinds of pension, at different times over the past 30 years and more. What matters is to do justice, as far as possible, among all those individuals. One has to discard the idea of a simple, new scheme as soon as one discovers that whatever scheme of that kind one can devise, it will do justice that is too rough to be called justice at all.	.
There is another possible method of proceeding. This other method, which has weighty advocates, is to legislate to bring every old pension up to the amount which the individual concerned would be awarded as pension, if he were retiring today on the same record of service as he actually had. But, apart from any other considerations, this method, too, is seen to run into practical difficulties, which
1	am afraid are insuperable. We are concerned with more than a quarter of a century of turbulent, national history which has seen enormous changes in the organization of the various services with which we are dealing.
This quotation, sir, is all too true of our situation here. A flat percentage increase in all pensions to those retiring before a certain date would give a pensioner retiring just before that date an unjustifiable advantage over the person retiring just after that date, with the same service. In addition, even for those retiring at the same time there is the complication created by the fact that there are six different benefit formulae to be considered when determining what increase should be made in the pensions of the three groups which are under review, namely the civil servants, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the armed forces; because, depending upon the time at which the individual affected came under the relevant statute, he will have received a pension of
2	per cent of a certain salary, or average salary, over a certain period for each year of service up to 35 years.
As I have already indicated, the position is very much loaded in favour of the person who retires on the final salary or his last year's salary rather than on a salary under the 10-year average upon which most civil servants are at the present time. I think it will be agreed by the house that there is a strong argument for providing more than one series of adjustment factors. I think, Mr. Speaker, it should also be pointed out that this is one of several problems under the Public Service Superannuation Act for which consideration is now required.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and other hon. members have interested themselves in the problem of those who are under the retirement fund, who regrettably and

foolishly declined to elect to come under the Public Service Superannuation Act. Consideration must be given by the house to what extent we are to give them another opportunity to rectify what always was and what now appears even to them to have been a major error in judgment.
I do not need to refer, sir, to the problem of the employees of the soldiers' settlement board or the department of soldiers' civil re-establishment who were not considered permanent, and therefore were not under the 5-year average when it was in effect and are now under the 10-year average, because many columns of Hansard, as hon. members know, have been devoted to that.
These, sir, are but indications-and I see my time is rapidly drawing to a close-of the problem with which the new government was faced when it took office not yet six months ago. Immediately the new government gave instructions that the fullest possible review of all these superannuation problems be made by officers of the Department of Finance, the department of insurance and the advisory committee under the Public Service Superannuation Act. That has been going on and is going on today. It is only partially complete. Preliminary reports only have been made, reports of such a nature that a final decision cannot yet be made by the government.
As the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have stated in this house, this statistical and actuarial review will be completed at the earliest possible date, and an announcement of the government's decision will be made immediately thereafter. This is the assurance I can give to the house. There will be no stall, no attempt to avoid the issue directly once the basic facts, upon which a wise decision can be made, are fully known.
I hope, sir, that the debate on this subject today will serve a useful purpose. I hope hon. members on all sides of the house will try to help the government to achieve a fair and equitable solution of this complex problem. That the government will welcome and will give earnest consideration to all constructive suggestions from hon. members I can give positive assurance.
The brief to which the hon. member for Fort William referred a few minutes ago was presented to the Minister of Finance on November 15 by the civil service association of Ottawa, and copies of it were sent earlier to all hon. members. That brief is a helpful and constructive document and personally I want to congratulate the association and its officers upon the excellence of their presentation.
Now, sir, specifically I invite hon. gentlemen to express opinions, which I say would
Public Service-Pensions be helpful, as to whether there ought to be a single formula for the pension adjustment if adjustment is to be made, or ought there to be different formulae, varying as to the types of pension one from the other. If there should be an increase, ought there to be a ceiling placed on the increases as in the United States or the United Kingdom; and if a ceiling, at what figure and why? However, we have been brushed aside each year primarily with the argument that a contract had been made, that these civil servants knew what they were doing when they paid into the superannuation fund, and that the contract could not be changed now.
He went on to make it clear that that argument did not carry any weight with him, and I am glad the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has re-echoed that point of view today, in saying there are no insuperable barriers to dealing with this problem if the government of the day has the will to deal with it.
Last spring when we were debating a resolution similar to the one now before us, also on the motion of the hon. member for Fort William, the Minister of Public Works said, as found at page 1845 of Hansard of March 4:

This need should have been met a long time ago.
The Minister of Public Works was quite correct when he said last spring that the need should have been met a long, long, long time ago. Ten years ago it was under study in the department and the government

of that day promised to announce its policy as soon as it was decided upon. I hope we are not going to have to go through another 10-year period before getting action out of the present government.
May I say one or two other things by way of the history of this matter. Something of what I might have said is now not necessary because of what the parliamentary assistant has done by way of referring to the practices in the United Kingdom and in some of the provinces of this country. He has also referred to what has been done by the federal government in the United States. He might also have referred to the fact that in some of the individual states improvements have been made in the pensions of those already retired. There are a few instances in private industry where it has been done, both in the United States and in Canada as well as in some other countries. It is also true that in New Zealand and Australia steps have been taken to improve the position of those already retired. We can take action here, and I hope the house will accept the invitation of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance and make suggestions to the government so that action may be taken soon.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that in the main we have to divide this problem into two aspects. Perhaps they will have to be separated one from the other because the first one is more pressing. On the other hand there is the problem of the large number of people, retired civil servants and others, who are having to get by on very small pensions. Any attempt to build some new principle into the Public Service Superannuation Act to solve the problems that will arise in the future will not help those people who are on low pensions now.
I think the government is going to have to find some way to cut the Gordian knot and simply raise these pensions to a floor below which retired civil servants of the federal government should not be asked to live. So far as these people are concerned, I do not think the government should waste time trying to find some principle, some percentage formula. I suggest that there simply be established a floor below which no pension should fall so far as retired civil servants are concerned.
Perhaps at this point I might put some figures on the record. I shall read mine because there are very few of them. According to the last figures that we have obtained in the house, there were last spring still 393 retired civil servants drawing pensions of less than $20 a month. There was a total of 3,170, including the 393 to whom I just referred, drawing pensions of less than $50
Public Service-Pensions per month. Similarly, there were 1,248 widows of retired civil servants drawing pensions of less than $20 a month, and a total of 4,395 widows of civil servants drawing pensions of less than $50 a month. In the case of civil servants, those on pensions of less than $50 a month constituted, last spring, 22 per cent of all those drawing civil service pensions, and in the case of the widows the 4,395 constituted 64 per cent of all of those drawing pensions as widows of retired civil servants.
Even after we have dealt with the problem of those who are drawing these low pensions, pensions upon which people cannot be expected to live, there is the problem in terms of justice of doing something to improve the pensions of those who have enough to stay alive but the value of whose pension payments have been reduced or destroyed as described by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance.

speechtext:
Where some private employers have done that I have welcomed it as better than nothing, but I would not advocate it. To do that is to interfere with the basic principle with regard to old age security, that it is paid to everybody regardless of income, leaving it to the income tax to make any necessary adjustments. When you start taking into consideration old age security payments you create more problems than you solve.
I would prefer that what the hon. member has suggested not be done. There are other people with other kinds of income, people who are still working or who have investment income, whose private income is not interfered with by receipt of the old age security pension. We already have the case of the burnt out pensioner whose pension is interfered with because he receives old age security. I do not believe that should be the case, and I do not think we should extend
2430	HOUSE OF
Public Service-Pensions that principle into this field of the pensions of retired civil servants. In my view the universality of the old age pension is a good idea, and I do not believe we should interfere with it. In my view, if an employer has an obligation, as I believe he has, to provide a decent pension for his retired employee, that obligation is not taken away because of a state pension such as that provided under the Old Age Security Act.
I was about to make the point, Mr. Speaker, that not only do we have to be humanitarian and meet the plight of retired civil servants whose pensions are now in the lower brackets, but we have to consider the just claim of retired employees whose pensions might have been at reasonable levels at the time they retired, and see to it that the value of those pensions is kept up.
People have a right to receive enough to keep up with the cost of living. We go farther than that. We say that people have a right to receive enough, by way of pension, to keep up with a rising standard of living. After all, when people are retired any changes that take place in the economic levels are partly the result of the work they did in their working years. We do not believe that people, in their period of retirement, should be called upon to see the general standard of living rising while they have to tighten their belts and have life become progressively little more than mere existence.
We feel, therefore, that the whole Public Service Superannuation Act has to be looked at with a view to finding some formula whereby pensions can automatically be adjusted upward after employees have gone on those pensions.
Perhaps I could take this other half of the problem, as I was dividing it in the first place, and divide it into two parts. On the one hand there are hundreds, thousands, of retired civil servants now on pension, who right at this time may be getting a pension that sounds not bad when compared with these $30 and $40 pensions, but who feel that the value of their pensions has deteriorated since they retired.
In addition, there is the plight that will face some of our civil servants in the future, in that pensions which now sound adequate in due course will become inadequate. I have taken a quick look at one of these tables the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance placed on Hansard. It shows that if a civil servant retires today, after 25 or 35 years of service, he has a pension that is not too bad. I accept that. But do we not all know that five or ten years after such a person goes on pension


the cost of living may well have gone up? The standard of living, we hope, will have risen, and these people will find that the pension which sounded all right when they went on it will be inadequate.
I am going to come to this in a moment. I realize that this branches out into a much broader field than just the problem of civil service pensions, but for the moment let us deal with it in the field of civil service pensions. This seems to me to lend real support to the argument that has been advanced by some who have studied this matter that there should be built into the Public Service Superannuation Act a provision whereby once a person goes on pension at the rate determined by the formula in the act, that pension will rise automatically as the cost of living or the gross national product goes up across the years. I had a few things to say about this in one of the debates that took place on the matter in 1956. The suggestions I made, which I had gleaned through reading, of course, are to be found on pages 6107 and 6108 of Hansard for July 17, 1956.
I suggested, for example, that actuaries could ascertain, by studying the experience of the past, just how much the cost of living could be expected to rise during the period that a retired civil servant could be expected to live from the date of retirement to death. In other words, actuaries could ascertain in advance how much that pension should be increased year by year so the retired civil servant, during the years of his retirement, would have a fairly constant income in terms of its purchasing power in relation to the cost of living. This having been done, the government or parliament could make a decision as to whether those increases should be provided out of current revenue, year by year-and I think there is every justification for that-or the government and parliament might decide that what would be desirable would be a slight increase in the rate at which civil servants pay into the public service superannuation fund for the purpose of providing for these automatic increases in the years that lie ahead.
Another way, of course, is to have a separate fund altogether into which civil servants contribute so as to pay supplements to retired civil servants.
The quid pro quo in that case for civil servants being required to pay into such fund would be the knowledge that when they are retired, civil servants of that day would be contributing to a fund to increase the amount of their pensions at the time of their retirement.
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that these two main problems are of equal weight and

equal importance. I refer to the immediate needs of those on low pensions on the one hand, and to adjustments to take care of future inflation, on the other. We must address ourselves to both of them. But I urge that the government not let the time it might take to solve the second problem delay action on the first problem. Here you have these hundreds or thousands of retired civil servants and civil servants' widows with pensions that are inadequate. The time it would take to work out a new formula to look after future retired civil servants is such that if the situation is allowed to go on, these people will suffer unduly.
I therefore urge that the two problems be separated and that something be done right now by way of establishing a floor for pensions of those in the lower brackets. When they have done that, let the government not think that ends the problem. I say again to the government that there is no use boasting about the fairly decent level of pensions that people can now retire on, and forgetting that in the course of time, unless something is done, these rates of pension will also become inadequate.
It seems to me that the only way this problem can be met is to build into the superannuation plan some arrangement for an automatic increase in the pension as the cost of living goes up, or as the standard of living goes up, or both. It appears that there are times when we look exclusively at the cost of living in relation to these matters. No one denies that old people should have sufficient pension to meet the rising cost of living; but I think in this age when we are becoming, I hope, a bit more humanitarian, we should learn that older people have not only the right to sufficient pension to meet the rising cost of living, but that they should have sufficient pension to enjoy or participate in a rising standard of living as well.
May I say, Mr. Speaker, that the argument we are advancing with regard to civil service pensions applies not only to those which come in that category, including the mounted police, the armed forces and the Canadian National Railways-let us bring them in as well-but it raises the whole question of the need for some rethinking about pensions generally. There is on the part of some a tendency to wage certain battles and then, after those battles have been won, to feel that nothing more needs to be done. There are some who feel that perhaps enough has been done in the field of pensions generally. I suggest that we are just moving into a time when we are going to have to face another whole problem with regard to pensions.
For a moment, if I may be permitted to do so, I am talking with regard to a field broader
Public Service-Pensions than just civil service pensions. There was a day, for example, when my predecessor, Mr. Woodsworth, had to stand up in this house and argue against terrific odds that there should be an old age pension. It was a long battle. Eventually that battle was won, and it became established that it was right for the state in certain cases to pay an old age pension. The battle moved on. In due course the issue became not just the paying of a pension but the paying of a pension without a means test. For the first number of years that some of us were arguing for the abolition of the means test we were met with the argument that this was ridiculous, that this could not be done, that this would break the treasury, and so on. Yet eventually that battle was won, and we have established the principle of a universal pension.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the problem we are discussing today brings to our attention the realization that we are moving into a new field, that the time has now come when we must not only pay pensions to our older citizens, not only pay them on a universal basis, but must provide for those pensions to be adjustable, for those pensions to increase automatically so that people generally can meet the rising cost of living and participate in the higher standard of living.
We hear this suggested by some who argue that the old age pension, for example, should be adjusted according to the rise in the cost of living. We contend that is not enough. We contend that you must meet these other factors, the rise in the gross national product and the rising standard of living, as well.
I appreciate the fact that you did not call me out of order, Mr. Speaker, because I got away from civil service pensions into this broader picture, but I was doing it because it seems to me that what we are dealing with today is an issue that is of concern not only to retired civil servants, but is of significance to the country as a whole. To the argument which the hon. member for Carle-ton has very properly dismissed-and I am glad he did so-by saying we cannot do this because it would be a matter of discrimination against other Canadians, the answer I would make in reply is that this would be a case of giving a lead in this other field. In other words, if in the field of civil service pensions we can first of all establish the principle of a floor below which no pension should be allowed to fall; and if, in the second place, we can provide for pensions to be increased automatically after retirement to meet changing conditions, that will be giving a lead in the field of pensions generally, and it may be that this will be the beginning

Public Service-Pensions of our moving into a better era in so far as pensions and retirement allowances are concerned.
It has been a long battle, both in this specific field of civil service pensions, and in the general field of pensions to get this principle of old age security established. It has been a long, hard battle. The victories have been won rather slowly, but we have made headway to this point. We contend that what we are discussing today is a very important aspect of the matter into which we are now moving, and that is the desirability of having all pensions put on such a basis that they will increase after retirement in order to enable people to meet the rising cost of living and participate in the rising standard of living that is made possible by the sweat and toil of our people, made possible indeed by what those now retired have contributed in their working years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to congratulate the hon. member for Fort William not only for his willingness but indeed his determination to stick to his resolution until he sees some daylight. I consider it a pleasure as well as a duty to speak to this resolution which the hon. member for Fort William has presented, and which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were retired, after long service, when salaries were low, so as to bring their pensions in line with those of the present.
I want to say that I think those pensioners, and a mighty fine class of people they are, deserve some consideration. I want to congratulate the hon. member for Carleton, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, for the fine way in which he presented the argument on behalf of the government. If my memory serves me correctly I think that was his maiden speech in this house. I congratulate him on it. He has a fine speaking voice, is clear in his explanations and presents a mighty good argument. However, if he were in the opposition I think perhaps he would have taken a more positive view of this resolution and would not have submitted so much in a negative attitude.
Outside of those representing constituencies in the city of Ottawa, I think perhaps I have more retired civil servants in my riding than any other member in this house. The thing I find is that these people are now finding it mighty difficult to get along, because their expenses are far beyond their income. As the other hon. members who have spoken have pointed out, namely the hon. member for


Winnipeg North Centre and the hon. member for Carleton, the devaluation of the dollar has caused them quite a bit of concern.
I found out two or three things while visiting these homes, Mr. Speaker. In the first place, I found that these pensioners are not greedy; they do not have the attitude that the government owes them a living; they do not have this "gimme, gimme" spirit that some people have. But they take the attitude that they should at least receive some appreciation for work they performed under previous governments. As I say, these people are not greedy. I think the greatest characteristics of greed are devastating and conquering. I do not think these people showed these characteristics, at least not during my conversations with them. They are now finding themselves in a very serious situation as a result of having to meet an ever-increasing level of municipal taxation out of a fixed income.
I found, Mr. Speaker, that these people are living in continuing fear. Someone has well said that one of the greatest evils of fear is fear itself. These people fear today, tomorrow, next week and next month. I think this government could do nothing better than relieve this fear, because so much continual fear and worry is driving many of them into trouble, and putting many of them on their sick beds.
I found, while visiting these people, that they do not try to be aristocrats, although in my opinion a lot of them have earned the right to aristocracy because as fine civil servants they were a credit to the government for which they worked, a credit to their country and now a credit to the municipalities in which they live. They want to hold up their ends, if I may use that expression, in their municipalities, but they are limited, as I say, by their difficulty in keeping up with ever-rising levels of local taxation. Nevertheless, they want to make those municipalities better places in which to live, and I think their efforts deserve a wealth of consideration.
One civil servant to whom I spoke told me he had heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) express at different times the opinion that the pensioner should receive more as prices rose. Indeed, I listened to the Prime Minister speaking over the radio from Toronto when he said that a Conservative government would raise the amount to a figure high enough to meet the needs of recipients, with subsequent adjustments tied to the cost of living. Then again, in a television broadcast on May 22, he amended this

proposal to make it more specific by this promise and I quote:
We Intend to fix a fair and reasonable amount for the old age pensioner and, indeed, for the other pensioners, and also to make provision for a formula whereby due allowance will be made in the future for the rising cost of living.
And I well remember listening to election speeches made by the Prime Minister during his campaign when he stated on different occasions that it was time to take the unrepentant tax masters off the backs of the Canadian people. Well, we now have an opportunity to do this and I hope the government will acquiesce in the resolution so well presented by the hon. member for Fort William urging us to do something with regard to this problem and certainly by voting for this resolution we would be showing a spirit of reciprocity in the light of the work these retired civil servants have done so well on behalf of the government.
Mr. Speaker, at this time of the year, with Christmas coming close, we all know that the spirit and the theme of Christmas are based on the words "Peace on earth, goodwill towards men", and I say this, regardless of the political affiliation of any member of this honourable house, I think it is the duty- and I am not a minister-of every one of us to remember in our prayers each day the deliberations now taking place in Paris, and pray that we may see peace and unity in the years to come.
I appeal to the government to carry out the second part of this Christmas theme- good will towards men-and I am sure that if they would do something with regard to this resolution it would certainly make these people very happy, remove fear and anxiety from their homes and make their declining years upon this earth far happier than they are at the present time by giving them some assurance that they could at least meet the rising cost of living. If we could approve of this resolution I think we could throw back our shoulders and thrust out our chests with justifiable pride because we would have helped at least one class of people who performed their duty very well in the past on behalf of the administration of Canada in this wonderful service.
Mr. Speaker, what a wonderful Christmas present it would be if the government would announce that they intended to do something immediately with regard to increasing pensions paid to retired civil servants. I hope the government will act soon and that it will not wait too long for the report which the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance has mentioned. Action is needed right now, not tomorrow or next
Public Service-Pensions year. These people are suffering, and it is up to hon. members of this house to do something on their behalf. I hope every effort is made to relieve the conditions under which many of our retired civil servants are living at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, other hon. members who have already spoken have dealt in the main with the subject of pensions paid to retired civil servants but have not dealt at any length with pensions paid to former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and others. I should like to say a few words this afternoon in connection with the pensions paid to former members of the R.C.M.P.
I understand that this is the first time the subject of these pensions has been included in the resolution, and it gives me great pleasure to say something about it. When I began to do some research into this matter I thought the best place to begin would be by looking through the mounted police magazines and bulletins. The mounted police veterans association have a magazine, and most magazines of this type have columns and articles devoted to complaints or, at any rate, to drawing the attention of the public to various difficulties. I went to our splendid library and looked up a recent issue of Scarlet and Gold which is a publication of A division of the R.C.M.P. veterans association. I also looked at the R.C.M.P. Quarterly, and the commissioner's annual report because I thought that somewhere in these publications I would get a fairly good idea of the situation of the mounted police retired veterans. But in none of these publications I have mentioned-and I looked back over quite a number of years-did I find any complaint or article referring to pensions. I read of the historic deeds of members of the force in the early days; I read stories about the activities of the mounted police at the present time, crime detection methods, jokes on the police and so on, but nothing about pensions. The R.C.M.P. Quarterly also has an old-timers' column, which I read, and I found that all it contained was news about reunions, stories of the past and reminiscences.
Mr. Speaker, I could only conclude after going through all these articles that either there is nothing to complain about, or else the members of the force both present and retired are carrying on their great tradition of duty without complaint. After looking into the matter, I feel that the latter is the case-the R.C.M.P. is not going to air complaints in public. In fact, there is provision in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act

Public Service-Pensions forbidding the members of the force from laying complaints except through their own organization and superiors.
For that reason I have a great deal of pleasure in bringing to the attention of the house some of the problems relating to retired members of the R.C.M.P. and their dependants. While the mounted police themselves do not seem to be unduly preoccupied with the question of pensions an examination of the statute indicates that this house and those members of it who framed the original act were definitely concerned. The record of the service, the desire to attract able and qualified men as recruits and to maintain a high standard of service led to the establishment of a complete and complicated system of pension.
The act setting up the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and its pension scheme is found in the Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, chapter 241. In this act there are 115 sections and of these sections 43 deal with the establishment of the force itself and 72 deal with pension matters. The very distribution of the sections of the act seems to indicate that the original legislators were concerned with this question. Two-thirds of the act deals with pensions for officers, constables and their wives and orphans and if that was the intention at the time the act was set up and the force was established I believe it should be no less our intention and concern today.
I think it must be assumed that it has always been the desire of this house to provide the personnel of the mounted police with a certain freedom of mind as to their retirement and as to the care that will be given to their widows and children if they suffer accident or death in the service and sufficient funds for themselves upon retirement or injury. This well drafted provision has now become slightly out of touch with present day conditions. The basis of the difficulty is easy to locate and I think it is rather in the same line as the general pension plan of civil servants. The basis on which mounted police officers and constables are given a pension is the pay and allowance they receive during the last year of their service and therefore if they retired when service rates were considerably lower than they are now their pensions would be correspondingly lower.
I would like to mention at this point some of the provisions in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act. Section 67 of the act provides for the pension of a constable on retirement in the following language:
(1) The pension of a constable on retirement shall be,

(a)	if he has completed ten but less than 21 years' service, one-fiftieth of his annual pay and allowances during the last year of his service for every year of service;
(b)	if he has completed 21 but less than 25 years' service, an annual sum equal to twenty-fiftieths of his annual pay and allowances during the last year of his service, with an addition of two-fiftieths of such pay and allowances for every completed year of service above 20 years; or
(c)	if he has completed 25 years' service an annual sum equal to thirty-fiftieths of his annual pay and allowances during the last year of his service with an addition of one-fiftieth of such pay and allowances for every completed year of service above 25 years, but the pension shall not exceed two-thirds of such annual pay and allowances.
From this provision it is quite clear that the entire system is based upon his pay during the last year of service. This provision refers only to constables and section 44 of the act makes almost identical provision for officers of the force. The pension for widows and orphans is contained in another section of the act. This latter pension is somewhat different because while it is based on pay and allowances during the last year of service it is also made up partly of a contributory system. The constable during his service pays 5 per cent of his salary by way of deduction and the amount of the total accumulation of the deduction based upon his last year's pay and allowances forms the basis on which his widow and children are provided care. We can readily see from this that those retired members of the force who left the service some years ago and their widows and orphans are receiving pensions based upon rates of pay of perhaps five, ten or 15 years ago.
There was a general pay increase in 1956 at the same time the general civil service increases were granted. An examination of this pay rate indicates that it is a reasonable one and that the general pay and allowances of the mounted police, while they may leave something to be desired, are fair and equitable. This will work very well for those who are presently in the service and will be retiring following the granting of this increase but it will also work a hardship on those who are trying to get along on a pension based on what they made a few years ago. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) has stated that the matter is receiving serious attention on the part of the government not only with regard to the services and the R.C.M.P. but all other classes coming within the general scheme.
As is the case with all classes of persons in receipt of pensions, those in receipt of mounted police pensions have problems which are not simple to deal with. The first thing is that widows and orphans' pensions are contributory and therefore the basis of

payment is the basis of a contract. During his service a constable has paid into a fund, which has been set up, a percentage of his pay and when he retires from service or loses his life while in service the widow and children receive the amount which has accumulated and therefore this also raises difficulty with regard to other pensions. A contractual basis is there.
The government of Canada has agreed to assist R.C.M.P. veterans and they have agreed to accept such pay and the allowance as based on a contract. We have to consider to what extent the moneys of the general public should be used to increase an amount which was originally started off on a contractual basis. As pointed out by the hon. member for Carleton, other people who contributed to retirement allowances and similar schemes are not entitled by any stretch of the imagination to receive increases from the government merely because what they receive is lower than what is received by some one else. That is the first difficulty in meeting this particular problem.
The second matter which has to be considered is that many of the persons who are going to be particularly affected by an increase are those who retired some years ago. It would almost be safe to assume that most of those people would be within the old age pension bracket and we do know that at this session of parliament there has been at the public expense a general increase in pensions for all persons and those who come within the age 70 and older group have benefited as a result of those increases.
Then, there is also the 65 to 70 years of age group who may be receiving Royal Canadian Mounted Police veterans' allowances as well as old age assistance. There again, something is to be gained from a serious consideration and adjustment of the problem. There are also a number of people-and this is well known-who retired from the mounted police in what might be called the prime of life. If they entered the service when they were fairly young and served 20, 25 or 30 years and chose to retire, they did so with a reasonably good pension and they still have the opportunity of going into similar work. A good many of the chiefs of police in the smaller towns and persons of that kind are retired mounted police constables who gained a lot of experience in their service with the force. Those people have a regular income and probably they consider that their pension from the R.C.M.P. is in addition to that income and is something on which they can always fall back in case they lose their present income.
In Ontario and Quebec we have provincial police forces, but, except in those two provinces, the entire mounted police force do
Public Service-Pensions provincial duties as well as federal duties, which they were originally set up to do. Those who are relying mainly on their pension granted under the act referred to and who retired under the low rate are no doubt experiencing financial difficulty owing to the increase in the cost of living. Those are the people who must be considered. We must consider those who have no other source of income and who have suffered from the general increase in the cost of living.
I have not made any attempt to outline the great history and tradition of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and its predecessor the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, but in considering this matter we must remember that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are recognized the world over. They are a sort of badge of Canada. In addition to the maple leaf you see figures of the mounted police. In the minds of many people the world over they do represent Canada. Therefore, it is important-and it was the original intention -that the mounted police be kept on a high standard; that the pay and allowances be kept at a rate which will induce persons of high calibre to enter the force, and we should give them pension allowances which will remove from their minds any concern about their retirement. We must consider that they might take another position in life and probably earn a great deal more with a lot less hardship as an average citizen.
May I say just a few words about police duties generally. We all know, of course, that police duties are not the most pleasant in the world. In general, the police have the duty of carrying out the legislation which we pass in this house and which is passed in the legislatures of the provinces. Police duties involve those people who either wilfully or carelessly resist or ignore the laws of the land as they are established. At one time it was thought that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had to do only with policing the cold and vast hinterland of the north of Canada, and that their duties perhaps were not onerous except for the privations that they must endure and their obligation always to get their man throughout the snow-covered wastes of the northwest. Their duties have changed now. As I mentioned a minute ago, they carry out normal police duties in eight of the 10 provinces under arrangements with the various provinces.
We must consider this also in relation to the duties they must perform. The standard of conduct of the R.C.M.P. is very high. I mentioned a few moments ago the fact that a large number of sections of the act deal with the pension scheme of the R.C.M.P. and

Public Service-Pensions their dependants. In addition to that, one of the sections deals with no fewer than 24 offences which the R.C.M.P. constable may not commit and if he does commit them it may result either in his being arrested and fined or discharged from the service. These particular offences in the normal course of human existence in this country would not all be considered extremely serious; but the standard of service which is set in the act is high and the offences which they may not commit in service are very difficult to follow out.
In view of all these matters, Mr. Speaker, I do feel that very serious consideration should be given to the matter which is the subject of this resolution. I have not said anything about the civil service because it has already been very capably dealt with by hon. members who have made a serious study of the matter not only at the present time but over the years. The same rules should apply here as apply to the mounted police. This resolution is opportune and I think the mounted police pensions were well included. I am in favour of supporting this motion.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the stand taken by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), I do not see that there is much to be gained by using up the time of the house on this resolution. However, in the light of his request for information, we may be able to dish out a couple of points which may be of use to him when he really gets down to the consideration of this resolution.
Of course, his address was in many respects quite negative. I followed it as closely as I could and I did get the general impression that he was in favour of the resolution but how actively in favour or how enthusiastically in favour, of course, is another matter. You can be in favour of something, but in a case of this kind the people are aging and dying off and you can keep giving consideration to it and being in favour of it until the problem has solved itself. The hon. member gave acceptance to this resolution in just about the only manner in which the government could because, I am sure, that in the face of the debate which took place in March of last year the reaction could not be otherwise.
It is true he did not present many figures as has been done by past ministers of finance and departmental heads, and perhaps that too is in accordance with the words of the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), when speaking in the debate on March 4, 1957. As found at page 1856 of Hansard, he said:


I do not believe this house will be satisfied with listening to a lot of figures the Minister of Finance will put on the record later, perhaps only to show that it is going to cost this country a geat deal of money.
In the face of that I think the hon. member did about all that could be expected. He did not talk too much about money. He talked about the difficulties of working out scales and he made one statement to the effect that he did not feel the taxpayers' money should be used to assist a small minority as it might be an act of discrimination against larger classes. I think that was the meaning of what he said. I agree that all pensions have got to be reasonable. I do not believe in discrimination. I believe in fair play to all. On the other hand, we are dealing with a particular problem here and I think we might ask ourselves this question. Must this small group of pensioners be left to struggle and suffer, because the employer, in this case the government of Canada, did not provide a scale of pensions to meet their needs, while a plan is being worked out that will avoid any semblance of discrimination?
There is also the fact that in dealing with this question we are dealing with human values, values on which a dollar price tag cannot be placed. As I said earlier, I cannot see any need to spend too much time in deliberation and consideration in order to work out a scheme that from the financial point of view will be absolutely fair and actuarially sound. I agree with the suggestion put forward by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that in the meantime, in order that we may get on and meet the needs of these people in some way, a pension floor could be established. Some amount of money could be set as the minimum that would be payable to these people and action should be taken immediately to raise their pensions to a floor which will guarantee them a reasonable standard of living. I am going to quote another authority in support of that suggestion in the person of the present Minister of National Defence. As found at page 1855 of Hansard of March 4, 1957, he said:
If the government is not able to check inflation, then it seems to me only fair and just that the government must find some other means of helping those who are really the underprivileged class of the nation.
He is referring particularly to the deterioration in the purchasing power of the dollar. A few years ago $100 a month looked like a reasonable pension but we know how little the real value of that amount of money is today. Therefore I say that any floor that might be fixed as a matter of expediency and urgency should have regard to the cost of

living at the present time. That would be in keeping with the view of the Minister of National Defence in the remarks to which I have just referred.
I was also pleased to hear the hon. member for Carleton say that an adjustment is possible and that the matter is being given consideration. But I should still like to know whether the government is going to vote for the resolution and whether the consideration is going to be prompt or whether the matter is going to be stalled along for many years. When the present Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks) spoke in the debate on March 4, 1957, he said, as found at page 1860 of Hansard:
-unless the government takes action, nothing will be done this year just as nothing has been done in previous years.
We know that nothing will be done this year but we would have felt much better if the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance had assured us that their studies of the problem had reached the stage where they could assure the house that legislation would be introduced at the next session of parliament. Time is running out. After years of trying to eke out an existence on ridiculously low pensions, these people are finding it more and more difficult to finance their daily living. They are finding that under the present government just as under the former government the purchasing power of the dollar is shrinking daily and the problem is growing more acute. There is also the fact that many of these people are reaching the last stage of their life expectancy and I think it is high time that the government improved the treatment it has been handing out to them and raised their pensions at once so that in the latter years of their lives they may know something about what a reasonable standard of living can do for them. Many of these people are passing out of the picture altogether and, as I said, the longer the government waits the smaller the problem becomes due to the decrease in their numbers. I hope that prompt action will be taken and something will be done before the problem solves itself in its own way by these aged pensioners passing completely out of the picture.

I hope it will not be talked out, and for that reason I will not spend as much time as I would like on developing the question of the need of certain civil servants and pensioned R.C.M.P. for assistance. I take it that case has been made. Certainly as I was looking at the remarks of some ministers of the crown, I take it that it should not be necessary to convince the present government of that need.
The matter is somewhat complicated. There is no doubt about that, and no useful purpose would be served by trying to make it appear a simple matter. One of the difficulties I always found in working on the problem was that the statistical tables showing the average amount of superannuation being drawn by civil servants could be misleading. In some of the groups of low payments you would find persons who were receiving very low payments because they were superannuated before the pay increases had been granted and were, therefore, receiving very low pay. These persons, even though they had long terms of service, were suffering real hardship. In the same set of statistics you will often find a few who had been superannuated when they were quite young because of the abolition of their positions or for some other reason. They received a small pension because they had only worked in the service the required ten years and had not made it their care er. It is not quite good enough to just take the statistical figures as they stand, and argue the case from there.
The real hardship comes from the fact that there are many superannuated civil servants who were superannuated on the basis of earnings of the last ten years of their employment, but the date of whose retirement was prior to the date when pay increases became effective. For all practical purposes, pay increases in the civil service started about 1948. There were certain other increases, but for the purposes of this argument I shall ignore them. The pay increases started in 1948 and have continued during the years until now we have had two general increases in the last three years. This problem is not to be confused with problems relating to the superannuation rates that will be applicable to presently employed civil servants who will be superannuated in the future after having worked on the higher pay levels for the required ten years. This is a particular problem applicable to those civil servants who were superannuated on the basis of ten years' service before the pay increases were effective.
Because this problem arises in that way, it makes it somewhat difficult to find a general principle that will be applicable and that will

bring the desired relief. So far as I am concerned, relief there must be. I am inclined to think that the practical method of working out relief for those persons is not through waiting to amend the superannuation act by tying superannuation to the cost of living, but rather by seeking to make some direct payment to those former civil servants who, for the reasons I have mentioned and other related reasons, find themselves now unable to live on their superannuation.
That may lead the government into having to deal with them on a separate basis outside the superannuation fund. If in the study of this matter they find that it is necessary to do that, I would urge them to do so. The civil service superannuation fund is now on a good basis. The whole act was well administered and it is a very effective act. Indeed, the hon. member for Carleton, unlike his minister, was quite modest about the claims he made for the superannuation act. Having regard to any acts that I could examine and with which I could compare it,
I believe it is the best one that I have found. Certainly that was my experience, and over the years I have done a fair amount of work on it.
In seeking to cure this problem I would not want to have the government in any way weaken the act itself. On other occasions I may have something fairly sharp to say about' the failure of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) to support the civil service superannuation fund with the $50 million contribution proposed to be put in it by his immediate predecessor. However, I do not want to open up that subject now, other than to say that the civil service superannuation fund and the retirement funds that preceded it have been built up over the years. If you examine the history of them you will find that there were periods when they were in a very much weakened condition, or when they were not actuarially sound. As far as I am concerned, I want them to be brought on to a sound actuarial basis and kept there. A great deal has been done-and I think I can claim some credit for the former government for this-in putting that fund on a proper basis and indeed the whole superannuation legislation as it has developed since the superannuation act of 1924 and the basic amendments in 1944 and 1947. I think that is something for which the former government can claim a good deal of credit.
In meeting this problem, I hope it will be treated in such a way that the administration of the Civil Service Superannuation Act or the fund will not be impaired. But in saying that I want to make it clear that I am not in any way minimizing the need for action in

I do not think the number can be determined just by taking the statistical tables that have been given from time to time in answer to a question from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. However, the number is substantial.

It would be mere repetition on my part to say that I agree with the sentiments so well expressed by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) and that I welcome his assurance that some positive action by the government will be taken in the very near future.
I think, too, I can say that all hon. members who have participated thus far in the debate have resisted the temptation to make this a political issue, with perhaps the near exception of the hon. member for Ottawa West, which shows that the house feels it is in the best interest of these pensioners to proceed without conflict and see that some time in the New Year, or in the immediate future, some action will be taken.
It is not necessary for me to deal at length with the problem of the R.C.M.P. veterans and it is certainly not necessary for me to bring to the attention of a body of this nature the position which this group of veterans has occupied over the years, gained by their outstanding contribution to the development of Canada. I think we will all take for granted that this body of men, the veterans of the R.C.M.P., have done perhaps as much as any unit, or organization or body to contribute to the early growth of this country through the policing of vast areas of Canada in many difficult circumstances. We accept the fact, also, that they did this work at a time when they were surrounded by extreme hazard and at a time before hazard pay and allowances were known. We accept the fact that many of these men discharged their duty at extreme risk to themselves personally, and, of course, as many were career policemen made great personal sacrifices. I think I can say, in addition, that we will remember that the standard of pay which this country gave the force in those days was perhaps-and this may be the understatement of the year -not in keeping with the work which they were called upon to perform at that time.
Let us accept that all this is generally agreed, and let us look to see what has happened since that time. Like the hon. member for Ottawa West, my main concern in discussing this matter is that since pensions were first awarded many of these men now find themselves in a very serious financial
Public Service-Pensions position unless they are able to supplement their income by means of some other employment. It has been mentioned to us here that many of them do perform useful functions at the present time. In fact, I have heard this used as an argument why an increase in pensions should not be awarded to them, but I think hon. members will agree that this factor should not disqualify them from receiving an increase, or handicap them in any way, because if we are realistic we must realize that if a man has not enough to live on and pay his bills he is bound to take some other employment.
On one occasion a former minister of finance said, in justification of not awarding increase in the payment made to these veterans, that the pension was never intended to maintain them, but only to supplement their incomes. But I think the hon. gentleman who said this, if he was here today, would agree with us that in the light of the declining purchasing power of the dollar the value of the award should at least remain constant, and that these gentlemen should not be placed in an unfortunate position merely because they gave their service at a time when the rates of pay were not high. There has been a suggestion to the effect that any increase in the pensions might establish a precedent which would create problems for a government in the future. It is interesting to note that two increases were granted to them, one in 1927 and a second in 1930, but it is equally significant to observe that it has been 27 years since government consideration has been given to increasing pensions for this particular group of men.
It is important to remember that any lengthy delay in recognizing the need for increasing pensions for this group will result in many of these men being deprived of the increase through death. An examination of the figures indicates that there are very few men in this special group who are alive today. The cost of increasing pensions for this particular group who came under the old scheme will not be large by virtue of the fact that in approximately ten or 15 years, based on the mortality rates, many of these men will not be with us. It therefore seems imperative that we should act quickly in recognizing the service these men have given through increasing their pension without delay. As the hon. member for Ottawa West said, the need for increasing the pensions of this group is perhaps more urgent than that of any other group who are in receipt of pensions under consideration in this resolution.
The actual pay of R.C.M.P. officers has increased, I think, by something like 70 per cent over the last six years and I maintain

The hon. member for Carleton has asked for some advice as to how this could be implemented and how actual income could be related to an increase in pension.
