Certainly our retired civil servants, R.C.M.P. and C.N.R. employees should not be told that they are the exception to the rule. I take my seat believing that the government will act on its stated

intention and give immediate consideration to this matter so that the needs of the people for whom I have made my case specifically can be attended to as urgent business.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this resolution I should like first of all to compliment the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) for his perseverance and persistence in presenting this resolution year after year as he has done. I have supported it on previous occasions and I rise to do so again today. I should also like to compliment the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) not only for the very lucid explanation which he gave of the difficulties that would have to be overcome in implementing this resolution but also for the very sympathetic attitude he displayed toward it. The hon. member for Fort William rested his case on two arguments. One was that justice demands it and the second was that necessity requires it. To these I should like to add a third argument, the argument of the necessity of the government accepting the moral responsibility to live up to its contracts.
The hon. member for Carleton said that the government should be a model employer and I agree with him wholeheartedly in this. We all know that the predicament in which retired civil servants find themselves today is due mainly to two factors. One is that their pensions are low, and they are low because salaries at the time of their employment were low. I think it is well known that over the years civil service salaries generally have been much lower than those paid for the same services and responsibilities in comparable jobs in industry and commerce; but civil service salaries were low because the salary itself was only part of the contract. The other part was represented by security. When a civil servant became employed in service he did so with the understanding that his salary was going to be lower than what he would receive for comparable work in industry but on the other hand he was going to have a certain amount of security during his retirement years. The second factor is that that security has not been provided and it is the moral responsibility of the government to provide it as quickly as possible.
There are three reasons why civil service pensions are not adequate to meet the increasing needs of pensioners. One is that continued inflation has depreciated the value of the dollar almost continously over a great many years. The second reason is that the pension, at the time it was calculated, was geared to the living standards of that day

and we all know that living standards have improved considerably every year and will continue to improve as the years go by. The third reason is that, along with rising standards of living, we have had a continued rise in the living costs.
The hon. member for Carleton solicited suggestions as to how this problem should be met. In my opinion these three factors must be taken into consideration when the solution is being worked out. Since the dollar has depreciated roughly at the rate of 3 per cent per year, to restore the purchasing power of the pension it should be increased by at least that amount, 3 per cent per year for the number of years the pensioner has been retired. Then, there should also be a clause to make sure that under no circumstances will the pension remain below the subsistence level. The third factor should be an extra bonus, included in the formula, to compensate for the increase in living standards over and above the living standards of the period to which the pension was geared.
During this session we have already taken action to alleviate the condition of our old age pensioners. We have treated them on an emergency basis on the assumption that the people concerned could not actually live without an increase in their pensions. We have justified the pension we have given to those old age pensioners, as a matter of right, on the basis of their contribution to the general economy of the country during their working years and on the assumption that today we are enjoying the fruits of their labour. We must remember that the civil servants also made their contributions to the economy of the country in the same way as every other worker did, and for that reason they are entitled to the same consideration as we would give to old age pensioners and other groups whom we have assisted with benefits during this session. But, on top of that, not only have they given their contribution to the economy, they have made a contribution to their retirement in two ways. One of the ways is by a direct contribution to the superannuation fund, but they made it in another way by accepting a much lower salary than they could have received outside of the civil service in comparable positions in industry and commerce. Therefore, they have a triple claim to our consideration and their case should be treated with the same urgency as we have treated other pensioners.
I would therefore suggest that action be taken at this session. I think a rough calculation can be made and the terms can be worked out afterwards. Some allocation should be included in the supplementary estimates at
Public Service-Pensions this session so that the government can discharge its moral obligation to those faithful old servants. Action on this obligation has already been too long delayed.

Mr. Speaker, once again a resolution comes before us for the consideration of the civil servant who is on pension and who perhaps was retired some years ago when the cost of living was considerably below what it is today. Once again we have heard some speeches similar to those we heard in days gone by. Once again I rise to support the resolution which stands in the name of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I do wish to pay the hon. member a compliment and I believe we all should. We should express our appreciation for his bringing this resolution before the house consistently year after year. It reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation to increase the pensions of civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were retired, after long service, when salaries were low, so as to bring their pensions in line with those of the present.
I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government would see fit to pass this resolution and bring in legislation in the very near future, for I believe that if the hon. member for Fort William is to retire later on-we all hope he might return to the house-it would be a pleasant thing for him to be able to retire and know that in his honour perhaps- if I can put it that way-legislation had been passed to increase the pensions of civil servants. I think that would be something that would give him a good deal of satisfaction. Since he is a veteran of this house, it seems to me we could very well honour him in this respect. When a man retires it is pleasant for him to know that he has some sort of memorial that he can leave behind. In the case of the honourable member, a piece of legislation that has helped those who have been the unfortunate victims of policies that have not kept pace with the rising cost of living.
We support this resolution, Mr. Speaker, because we recognize it is just; we recognize it is fair; we recognize it is the thing to do.
I do not think there can be any arguments against it. I should like to see it go much farther. Of course, governments have no responsibility in respect of the increase in pensions in other fields, but they do have responsibility for the amount of pension which is paid to civil servants. In the past I have talked with a number of people not civil servants who have had to retire on industrial pensions. I was out to the west coast a year or two ago and I happened to

Public Service-Pensions visit West Vancouver. It is a very fine community in which I found there were quite a number of retired people. I held one or two meetings while I was there and almost invariably some retired gentleman, mostly retired bankers, I must say, would come to me and ask if something could not be done about increasing their pensions. I mention this because it is apropos of the whole subject. A banker usually retires on what might be considered a fair pension. Banks have pension schemes and when bank managers retire they are supposed to retire with some considerable dignity, something that is commensurate with the position they held. Some of these old retired bankers find that their pensions have diminished in purchasing power far below what they ought to be and they cannot live in dignity any longer. That is something to be considered.
All this arises for one reason. The monetary policy of the country has been such that it has permitted the purchasing power of the dollar to become less and less as the years pass by. I have felt that perhaps it might be advisable to have some sort of escalator clause in all pension schemes whereby when an increase in the cost of living takes place the escalator clause will become operative. I am not prepared to say that it 'would be easy to write such a provision into a piece of legislation. I think it would require a terrific amount of research in order to accomplish it. However, under the present monetary policy that would be the fair thing to do because the combination of the depreciated dollar and the increased cost of living is something that is important to the living standards of the people of Canada who are on pension.
We who have been in public life for the last couple of decades recognize the importance of this matter. Civil servants who were retired some years ago were able to go to the grocery store and purchase enough groceries to make them feel that perhaps they had a fair pension. But when we consider the amount of their pensions in the light of the quantity of groceries they can buy today their pensions are pretty small because they will not buy very many groceries.
I had occasion at one of my meetings to have a chart indicating the amount of groceries that $10 would buy about 20 years ago compared with the amount of groceries of the same type that $10 will buy today. If you look at that picture it is a pretty grim one. Twenty years ago I suppose a man could buy a suit of clothes for $25 to $30, but go to your tailor or to a department store today

and see how much you have to pay for a suit of clothes. A person is lucky if he can get a suit less than $65 and they run from there up to $100.
Take the matter of shoes. Some years ago a man could walk into a store and get a pretty good pair of shoes for about $4 to $6 but if you go into a store today and try to buy a pretty good pair of shoes what do you have to pay? You have to pay considerably more. I have a pair of shoes on my feet for which I paid $19, and I do not think they are particularly exceptional. Of course, being a small man I think I should get clothes and shoes cheaper than a bigger man because there is not as much leather goes into my shoes or cloth into my clothes as in the case of a bigger man, but I do not get any consideration in that respect. My clothes take about half as much wool cloth but I have to pay just as much for a suit.
When we think of the depreciated dollar and the cost of living for the pensioner today compared with a few years ago I say that that should give the government a terrific amount of concern. When the hon. member for Fort William introduced the resolution this afternoon he talked in terms of an allegory. He spoke of a shotgun hold-up. It is a good allegory indeed. If somebody should come up to you, stick a gun in your ribs and take half the contents of your pocketbook away from you you would say that was robbery and everybody would be out to catch the robber and put him in jail.
But let us follow the illustration further. Suppose a man now on pension was able to save a little stake during his working years which he thought he would be able to use in future years. Suppose he bought $5,000 worth of bonds or put $5,000 in the bank some years ago. Suppose he cached away in one form or another bonds or savings to the extent of $5,000 15 or 20 years ago. Suppose he takes the money out of the bank today and attempts to live on it. What do you suppose he is going to get for it? He is only going to get half what he would have got some years ago. In other words, the purchasing power of the money that he put away, whether in the form of savings, bonds or in a pension scheme, is only half as much today as it was before.
Somebody robbed him. Who was it who robbed him? He is not at present sitting on one of the front benches of this house. You cannot very well put him in jail, but certainly if somebody robbed with a gun you would put him in jail. That is where he belongs. He is a criminal. But what has happened? A financial policy which controls the amount of money in circulation and has

an effect upon business-you can use what terminology you like; you can talk about inflation, deflation, or whatever you wish- has affected the cost of living. What has happened? The financial policy of the country has stolen half the pensioner's savings. That is a fact.
Who has been responsible for the financial policy of the country which has robbed the civil servant of half his income? Somebody is responsible for financial policy. The resolution advocates that mounted police pensions should be raised. I think we should bring in the mounted police for another purpose. We should bring them in to track down the real criminal so that we can put him in jail. If it happened to be the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) we would say to him, "Here, how is it that you have robbed the retired civil servant?" Oh, I know what he would say. He would say, "I have not robbed him of anything".
Somebody is in charge of the financial policy of the country. My hon. friend says, blame the Liberals. I think we could blame the Liberals because over the last 20 years they have been the ones who have been in charge of monetary policies. If they have not been in charge of the monetary policies of the country, then they had better say so. If the present finance minister is not in charge of the financial policies of the country, then he had better say so. If he says so, then we had better find out who is in charge of the financial policies of the country.

Yes, and I am glad my friend, the hon. member for Vancouver East, backed me up in that question to get something more from the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker).
The parliamentary assistant gave us a very excellent, well thought out speech this afternoon. He must have spent quite a bit of time in studying his subject, and we appreciate that. During his speech he referred to the previous finance minister and the attitude of that minister to the effect that you should not tax all the people to pay certain classes of pensioners who have been penalized by the decrease in the value of the dollar. Those are not his exact words, but that is the sentiment. I agree with that to some extent, but the irony of it is that the Minister of Finance, under whose department civil service pensions come, is the very man who sets the monetary policy of Canada which causes the value of the dollar to decrease. Now he turns around and says we should not tax everybody in Canada to pay one section of Canada's pensioners because they are unfortunate in the devaluation of the dollar.
However, the very government that is in charge of the civil service is also in charge of monetary policies throughout the country. The parliamentary assistant has stated that the government would give earnest consideration to all constructive suggestions. So far as I can see there are only two constructive suggestions. The first suggestion is to take the bull by the horns and raise the pension; that is about the best suggestion I could offer in view of present monetary policies. I am hoping the government will not delay taking action. Let us not have a lot of window dressing in this matter. Over the years we have heard a lot about the government being interested in anything that is for the benefit of the people of Canada. I know the government is because they are human like anyone else.
What we want is action now. The best assurance we can have of your sincerity and faith is that you take action now and not leave it for another ten years. This thing has been going along for a good many years now. We have been talking about this matter in this house for a good many years and it is time that some action was taken.
The other suggestion I have to make is this. Perhaps it would be a little bit more complicated, but I believe the government owes it to the people of Canada today to set up some sort of committee. I am not saying that they should set up a commission; this country is going to be burdened with commissions. I

believe they should set up some sort of committee-we have a regularly constituted banking and commerce committee of the House of Commons-to go into a detailed study of the reason for the higher cost of living as it is reflected in monetary policy. By that I do not mean a committee or commission on price spreads. That is a very simple thing. It does not take into account the fact that there may be something wrong with monetary policy. Let the government have the banking and commerce committee go into a real study by calling in the bankers, the financial experts, the monetary reformers, the people who have any understanding of monetary policy whatsoever, with a sincere desire, not to protect a faulty policy, but to try to arrive at the reason why this present financial policy is not working.
I do not think I need to have anything more to say on that matter. I was talking with my colleague the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) who is my desk-mate. He said to me, "You can raise the pension, something which would be a very good thing; but in the end it is only putting a patch on the old tire, because if you do not get to the root and the bottom of the trouble that is causing the tire to blow out, you will only have another blowout a little bit later on". Let us stop this patchwork business and let us get down to solid rock bottom in our effort to discover the reason why there is in the cost of living a fluctuation that is far too severe. Then we shall not have this repeated dog eat dog performance, because just as soon as you give some benefit to one, you have to give it to another and then some other organization comes along; everybody is out for his share, and there is not enough to go around under present monetary policy.
I will not say any more. The resolution should be passed. The problem should be solved. Since we now have a new government let us look forward in the hope that this new government is going to take some action to solve this problem, that it is going to be agreeable to the passing of this resolution and to hasten the legislation which will make the resolution effective.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a certain amount of deference that I venture to disagree with a member of such wide experience and broad humanity as the hon. member for Fort

William (Mr. Mclvor), but speaking for myself, I find that his resolution is too narrow in its proposed application, and that it is therefore inadequate.
In the course of my every day business I am constantly advising people-widows and dependants of those who are subject to inadequate pensions-and I might say, in particular, ministers of the cloth and preachers. I am certain there is no class of people in this country who are less well provided for in the matter of pensions than retired ministers and their dependants. These are people with whom everyone must have great sympathy. Their problems are great, and there is no one to whom they can turn for help. I think that when we are dealing with the matter of inadequate pensions, we should, however, look further into the causes in order to determine the reasons and remedy them.
One of the reasons why the pensions granted to civil servants some considerable time ago are low in the light of today's circumstances is that the government was at that time in the forefront in providing any pension at all for retiring civil servants, with the result that these pension schemes were very often set up without adequate contributions being made either from the employer or from the employee.
I know further that there are thousands of people in Canada contemporary with the civil servants with whom we are now dealing who have no provision for pension whatsoever, and also that there are many whose pensions are even less adequate than those of retired government civil servants. This, I think, is the first cause of the -situation with which we are dealing now.
The second cause is the continual decline of the purchasing power of our money. The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) suggested that this was a problem which had risen only in the last 30 years or so. Well, not many days ago I was reading a biography of Oliver Cromwell, and in that biography was a speech made by him some 300 years ago in the British House of Commons. The subject matter of that speech was the relationship of wheat prices to the purchasing power of the English currency at that time, and with a slight modernization of phraseology that speech could well have been made in this house last week.
There are many more people suffering from inadequate pensions than those covered by this resolution-teachers, librarians, municipal servants. In my own experience in municipal affairs I have many times had to deal with municipal employees pensions which were entirely inadequate to meet the need.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the present government and, indeed, the former government,
Public Service-Pensions have not been entirely unaware of this situation. Four times at least the problem of inadequate pensions and inadequate incomes resulting from the decreased purchasing power of our currency has been faced by the government. It was twice dealt with by the late government; first, when the universal old age pension without a means test was introduced and then later in 1957 when they increased the universal old age pension by $6. The situation has been twice faced by the present government; first, when the $9 increase in the universal old age pension was put into effect just recently and, secondly, in the undertaking by the present government to have a complete investigation made of a social security program for all our people based on need and the cost of living.
With all due deference to the hon. member for Fort William, I think that therein lies the real solution of the problem, because in my opinion, as the resolution stands, it is discriminatory. I think it is better to face the whole problem in a comprehensive fashion rather than to deal with one inadequacy and then to be faced with another.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate to this house the general sympathy which has been evoked by the motion of the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). We were entertained in some way this afternoon by some of the statements he made in his rather powerful appeal to our emotions. I know that in the past the hon. member has had some rather harsh things to say about tobacco and its use, but this afternoon we were treated to some powerful words on just what sort of man we would have if he were deprived of his pipe. I feel the hon. member might have chosen some other thing of which to imagine a pensioner deprived rather than his pipe.
Seriously, the hon. member showed briefly but movingly some of the hardships which have fallen to the lot of some of our retired civil servants, but I feel that those observations would apply with equal force to others who have retired on pensions of any sort. I would ask: does this not also apply to people who have retired on savings, on rent from properties, or on annuities, even government annuities? They have seen their savings disappear as a result of inflation and other causes. I do not suggest we should say, as is said in the courts, that hard cases make bad law but I rather think that the problem of our retired people is oversimplified and overemphasized at times.

Public Service-Pensions
There is, it is true, a great deal of hardship, but I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the hon. members of this house that the elderly people in Canada are not all in the same class. There are many people who have been frugal and who have saved, and they do not depend on pensions for subsistence. Indeed, if the conditions which have been indicated by the hon. member this afternoon were general, then this country would indeed be in a bad way because it would then appear that all our people who have reached the age of 65 or 70 have dissipated all they have ever earned in their productive years. Yet, Mr. Speaker, I know that that is not the case. We have groups of people, in varying percentages, who either because of circumstances beyond their control or because they have not been frugal enough or because they have been intemperate would now be faced with destitution if it were not for their pensions.
But, Mr. Speaker, that is not the general condition in this country and therefore I say that merely to emphasize the lot of these people and to point it up in eloquent terms such as we have heard may be somewhat misleading. We must deal with these particular cases. We have a responsibility and there I recognize the humanitarian interest of hon. members. We cannot let our neighbours be destitute. However, I am one of those who might take exception to what I consider to be somewhat of an oversimplification by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) when he spoke of the qualities of the ideal employer in that we are here singling out a particular group for treatment. There are many others in this position and I would suggest that the percentage of retired civil servants in this country who are dependent upon their pension as their sole means of subsistence is small compared to the rest of the retired population in this age group. What about those people who voluntarily put aside savings? What about those people who were not employed either by the civil service or in business where they might have been able to get a pension? What are we to do with them? They face the same problems.
I do not think it is right that we should consider only one group and consider all groups on a piecemeal basis. I feel we must give close attention to the entire question of retired civil servants, members of the police force and retired members of the armed services. Fortunately the number of retired service personnel is very few in number because before the war our regular armed forces were small in number. Nevertheless
these people face the same problems. I cannot say that all find themselves in this position because some have been frugal and have been able to provide for themselves in their retirement years. Whenever it can be done people should be encouraged to make provision for their retirement years. We should be most careful not to lead our people to the point of view where upon reaching retirement age they say to their employer or to the state, "Here I am; now keep me." I think that is wrong.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? Do I gather from what he is saying that he feels most people at age 65 or 70 who are in need are in that condition because they have not been frugal, not been temperate?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh no.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is
he taking the same position with regard to pensions that was taken in another place by a couple of hon. gentlemen?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Oh no, Mr. Speaker. I stated some time ago there may be circumstances completely beyond their control. I would say that the people who have not been frugal are probably the smallest number and fortunately so. I do not suggest for one moment that the people who are in need of their pensions today are in that position because they lacked frugality, but such people do exist. On the other hand there are people whose circumstances were such that they could not be expected to save to provide for their old age.
Including retired civil servants.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Then is the answer not universal pensions?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, I feel the answer is not universal pensions. While the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Carleton must be given weight I also feel that the position I have stated must not be disregarded. It must be considered in the whole problem of determining pensions for various groups.
While the government of Canada may be considered in the position of an ideal employer yet an ideal employer in providing pensions for his employees does so from his own funds or the earnings of his business, be he an individual or be it a corporation. In either case they use their own funds to provide pensions. In the present instance we are discussing the utilization of public moneys for the benefit of a particular group of people and I say we must consider this

in arriving at a solution to this problem. We have a responsibility not only to this particular group of people but to the people of Canada as a whole.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes, certainly.

Do you think that the
dominion government has any responsibility for civic pensions and teachers pensions? Do you not think we have dealt with the pensions for which the dominion government is responsible?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
At the moment I would not care to give the hon. member a categorical "yes" or "no" answer. I do not believe the question can be answered with a categorical "yes" or "no". However I agree to a large measure with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) who said that the low pensions we have today are in the main the result of low salaries that existed at the time these people were engaged and on which their pensions are based. I do not want hon. members to misunderstand me and conclude that I am opposed to the matter of inquiring into and increasing pensions where they are too low but I would like to draw the attention of the house to these factors which in my estimation must be considered in arriving at a just decision in these matters.
I would like hon. members to consider what might serve to alleviate some of the difficulties and remove the discrepancies which exist in the pensions which are the subject matter of this resolution and offer as a possible solution the suggestion of making a general change in the ten-year average by reducing it to a five-year average. The hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) indicated that there had been two rather substantial increases in pay in the civil service within the last two years. This has thrown the whole ten-year average scheme out of proportion. Those who retired over five years ago prior to these increases are now in receipt of the much lower pension because their base pay is proportionately lower. I feel there is true justification for inquiring into the situation prevailing in a particular group where there are discrepancies. You can readily understand that a civil servant who worked for 30 years received a pension of X dollars upon retirement ten years ago whereas a civil servant with the same number of years of service can retire today and receive X plus many dollars in the form of a pension. I do not think that is quite correct. I feel that the hon. member has a very good point in bringing the resolution forward at this time.
Public Service-Pensions
This proposal would certainly not take care of all the demands for increases in pensions of retired civil servants although, as I say, by removing some of the discrepancies and injustices within a particular group it would go to some considerable length in relieving the losses generally of those retired civil servants.
There are two particular items relating to retired civil servants about which I should like to speak. First of all, there is the subject which has been before this house on many occasions and, in particular, in 1953 when the superannuation act was under discussion here. It concerns a small group of civil servants who were members of the then department of soldiers civil re-establishment, the soldiers settlement board and treasury employees attached to the D.S.C.R. They are a small group of employees who are now in the main reaching retirement age. Because of some difficulties between government departments back in 1924 and 1925 agreement could not be reached that these veterans were permanent civil servants and they were still classified as temporary civil servants and were not able to elect as they should have been. Therefore, instead of being able to benefit from the 5-year average today they are unfortunately under the 10-year average. They never had a chance to elect through no fault of their own. I need not repeat the speeches that were made at that time by the Minister for Veterans Affairs (Mr. Brooks), the then leader of the opposition, the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness), and many others on both sides of the house, including the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). This is an anomalous condition which affects a number of men in my own riding and about whom I have made certain representations to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), and I hope that with a new look at the problem these men who have given very valuable service to this country, and particularly to the returned men, will be able to benefit and enjoy the same rights that their confreres in other departments now enjoy.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to a matter arising out of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the superannuation act. I have a constituent whose husband was a member of the mounted police back in 1922 when he transferred to the Alberta provincial police at its inception. One year later, during the discharge of his duty, he was shot down and died as a result of his wounds. There was then very meagre workmen's compensation legislation in our province. There were no pension provisions for members of the mounted police who died

Public Service-Pensions in the performance of their duties and this young widow had to fend for herself. For 32 years she has served as a special constable for the mounted police on escort duty under very arduous conditions. She has served as a matron particularly in the escort of mental patients, drunks, and what have you. This woman has been on call day and night over this period of 32 years. She is not on regular salary but is paid by the shift of so many hours per day's work. The mounted police authorities have been exceedingly kind and exceedingly considerate in keeping her employed in this way. Under workmen's compensation she drew the sum of $35 a month for many years. Now at the age of 67 she gets $60 a month.
However, last year, on her way to work one wintry night, she slipped and suffered severe injuries, breaking an arm or a shoulder. In any event, she has been incapacitated. Convalescence has been slow because of her age. She is not in condition really to discharge her duties as a police matron. After 32 years service there is at the present time no means of giving this exceedingly valorous and conscientious special constable, which she has been during all this time, a pension under the superannuation act. Mr. Speaker, I would humbly submit that such a case should deserve special consideration; that the people who are hired as special constables for a long period of time should somehow or other receive the same consideration as members of the force who are on a permanent basis.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that the principle of the resolution before us this evening is a good one, but I say that with this reservation. It covers a very small number of people, in fact, who actually are in dire necessity. I am not saying that a great number of people would not benefit by it and they would readily accept the benefit; but I say that when we are considering hardship cases we should not go from the particular to the general that because there are a limited number of cases we should apply the principle to the whole class. However, Mr. Speaker, I think the matter should be gone into as has been indicated by the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). I again congratulate the hon. member for Fort William for having moved this resolution so that we can discuss it here tonight.

Mr. Speaker, in rising for the first time to take part in the debates of this house I should like to take this opportunity, although I know it is late, to congratulate you and your deputy on the fact that you have been elected to your

high positions and also to extend congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) on appointing a lady to the cabinet of this country. I know the ladies in my own riding were very pleased with the promise the Prime Minister made that if he formed the government there would be a lady in the cabinet. I know they are very happy over the selection of the lady member and we know she will do an excellent job.
The people of Brantford riding have sent many men to this house and we have to go back some few years to the last Conservative member who represented Brantford riding. I refer to Mr. Ryerson who, although he is now 85 years of age, still takes a very active interest in the happenings in and the debates of this house.
I hesitated to rise in my place and speak in this house because I learned a long time ago when I was first starting in municipal work that it is a good plan to sit back and listen to the other speakers and learn something about the rules and regulations governing the debates and the work of this house. In speaking to this resolution which we are debating tonight I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) for the very splendid address he made this afternoon. It was very comprehensive and was certainly well thought out.
I would like also to say a word to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I only wish I had his mind and could retain all the details of which he is capable and had his ability to get up and speak on as many subjects and as often as he does.
Oh, no.

I would like to speak for a few moments on the question of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, this force of men of whom we are very proud in this country and which we know constitutes one of the finest police forces in the world. We are all conscious of the glamour of their uniform and we all remember the stories we read as shall I say younger boys; we remember the stories written about the force by Ralph Connor, "Corporal Cameron", and "The Patrol of the Sundance Trail" in which the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are glorified. We all enjoyed those stories and the episodes recounted in them.
I was looking through the report of the commissioner today and I have seen that there are not many instances detailed therein of the work done by the force and of their bravery. I was, however, struck by one or two of the men mentioned by the commissioner. We have Constable Johnstone who

entered a bank in response to an alarm and, after shooting three men, a fourth one came out and held up his hands. This constable was responsible for saving the money in that bank and preventing a hold-up. We also have another constable, Constable Ingalls, who received an award for saving a life in Gladstone, Manitoba. Then there is Sergeant Austin and Constable Ross who were highly commended for their excellent skill in aviation by taking an aircraft in flight and bringing it into Goose Bay, Labrador.
We have two more constables, McHale and Bowyer, who rescued a man from under tons of frozen gypsum and rocks at Windermere and also Constable Martin and Constable Millhouse who were commended for bravery they displayed during the flood operations in the Haney district of British Columbia.
It is therefore obvious that we still have men doing hazardous work in this force with very little publicity. The older men of the R.C.M.P. who did these valorous deeds in years gone by did not, of course, have the facilities of our men today. I am thinking of those men who used to be up north and who had to travel by dog team, by horse in winter and by canoe in the summer. Now we have modern equipment for them, airplanes, automobiles, helicopters. All of this is a far cry from the hardships which the older men endured when they looked after our far-flung borders in the north country.
I was fortunate enough to be able to procure information on half a dozen instances of the meagre pensions upon which some of these men had to retire. I have one instance before me of a man who gave 20 years service and who received a pension in 1937 of some $36 a month; another one who put in 14 years of service and received $34 a month; another constable who retired after giving 20 years service on a pension in 1929,-we all know, of course that 1929 was a peak year and had been for some considerable time, when wages were high,-but he was retired on less than $40 a month. Then we have another constable who gave 20 years service and in 1929 received a pension of $43; a sergeant who had put in 20 years service in 1928 was retired on $48 a month. Another staff-sergeant-somewhat higher in rank-having put in 20 years of service received $51 a month. So hon. members will see that a number of the older men who are still alive are today receiving these low pensions. They are certainly not burdened with a lot of money when it comes to pensions.
When considering the scale recently put forward for pensions payable in the R.C.M.P. under the Royal Canadian Mounted Police Act we notice that they have been considerably increased over the period from 1937 96698-156
Public Service-Pensions to 1957 and we agree that a constable or an officer of the R.C.M.P. who retires now is fortunate enough to receive a fairly adequate pension. He will receive one upon which he will be able to get along and look after himself, so I do feel that our older men should certainly receive the consideration of this house. They do deserve it and should be brought up to a point where they can live decently, without needing to go out and work after having given years of service on the hazardous work on which they have been engaged.
I know we are not discussing pensions other than those of the R.C.M.P. and the civil servants today but I wonder if I might be allowed to deviate for a moment. I am also concerned about the pensions in some of the industries in my home town. After all, these people of whom I am thinking are the ones who are paying the taxes in order to provide for the pensions we are discussing today. I mention in particular the textile workers in our city. These people belong to the poorest paid group in my city, due to the hard conditions under which the factories are running and the competition with which they are faced.
I am also concerned with the old age pensioners who, through no fault of their own, are living, and indeed have to live, strictly on the old age pension which we are paying today through the federal government, with the help of the Ontario government. In my experience in the municipal field I have had these old age pensioners come to me time after time wondering how they were going to pay their taxes, buy their groceries, pay for their fuel and live on the small amount available to them. Fortunately another promise of this government has been kept and they are now receiving a much better pension than they had a year ago or two years ago. It will certainly be a great help to them in order to enable them to buy the necessities of life.
The reason I mention these different groups is that no matter how much we reserve for these pensions for the civil service and the R.C.M.P. the money will have to come from one pocket only and that is the pocket of the Canadian taxpayer. No matter whether they are paying income tax, which we have been discussing recently, or not they still pay their share in other taxes such as sales tax, etc. I would suggest that thought and consideration be given by the government to these pensioners, bearing in mind that we all share in the cost thereof.

Mr. Speaker, I believe that this house owes a debt of gratitude to the hon. member for Fort

Public Service-Pensions William (Mr. Mclvor) for having persevered in bringing forward this resolution year after year. I do hope that the government will bring in legislation to take care of increases in the pensions of civil servants and the R.C.M.P.
Thank you.

I can think of no finer tribute that could be paid to a grand old man who has well and truly served his country and this house.
When I was first elected, Mr. Speaker, I received a letter which reads as follows:
When you go to Ottawa at the next session of parliament, I hope you will look into the plight of R.C.M.P. service pensioners-those who retired before the numerous increases were granted to serving members.
In my own case, I retired in 1947 on a pension of $82.40 per month, which in those days was not bad but now increased costs of living have made the pension insignificant, and I feel that all R.C.M.P. service pensioners under $100 per month are due for revision upwards.
I did see the commissioner and discussed this with him and he gave me the address of the veterans' organization for the R.C.M.P. They sent me a brief. In my opinion, the R.C.M.P. pension scheme is perhaps the most unsatisfactory pension scheme in existence. Going back to this same case, it concerns a man who joined the force in 1925, became a corporal and retired in 1947. His pension is twenty-four fiftieths of his pay, that is one-fiftieth for each year of service. In 1947, the pay and allowances for a corporal in the R.C.M.P. amounted to $2,060 per year, and this resulted in the pension of $82.40 mentioned before. Since 1947 normal increases have come about which, the brief says, amounted to 70 per cent but according to the information I received from the commissioner amounted to more than that. Today a corporal would receive in pay and allowances $4,800 a year, as compared with the $2,060 in 1947. The job is the same, the risk is the same, the qualifications are the same, but the man who served at the time when wages were low suffers now because of the low pension he receives. He gets it going and coming.
Under the present wage scale the pension would appear to be adequate, but the pension for those who retired in the early years is totally inadequate. The thing which amazes me is that when these advances were made in wages of the R.C.M.P., the government of that day did not amend the pensions in a similar manner. It would appear that if you were to tie the pension to the going rate of pay you would automatically increase the pension when the pay was increased. The trouble, of course, is that in industry you have collective bargaining between employees and employers. There is a continuous pressure

from the men for increases, and a withholding on the part of management to keep the increases at as reasonable a level as possible or as low as possible. In so far as civil servants and the R.C.M.P. are concerned, you do not have that force on the part of the men concerned because they are truly civil servants. They may submit briefs and so on, but they cannot take any more drastic action than that. It is, therefore, rather natural, although regrettable, that their wages lag behind the wages of other people across the country.
As I say, I think this illustration gives the picture in about as clear a manner as possible. When this man retired in 1947 the salary level was $2,000 and today people doing the same job are receiving $4,800. There is something wrong there. I was most interested when the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Mcllraith) was saying that there was no argument against this today. I would say there was no argument against it in previous years, either. I suffer from the handicap of not knowing what was said in previous sessions, so I do not know whether or not the previous governments took the fair minded attitude that has been taken by the government representative today, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell).

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The
previous government promised to study the matter.

Well, I would say it was a very lengthy study and did not do very much for the pensioners concerned. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) gave a few figures which struck me as being almost fantastic. He said there were 393 civil servants retired who would receive less than $20 per month pension and 4,395 widows who would receive less than $50 per month and that would represent 64 per cent of those who were pensioned. When you hear such figures as those, you know that the time is long past when this problem should be solved.
At the same time, however, one must remember that the government has had a very full program of legislation this session; that they have had a lot of work to do and a lot of getting used to, and you cannot expect, as the hon. member for Ottawa West seems to expect, that Rome can be built in a day or everything that is requested can be accomplished overnight. I sincerely believe that the government is considering this matter, and not with a view to bringing out a report but with a view to introducing legislation to correct this situation in a manner that will keep it corrected. How this will be

done I do not know, but it can be done. I am quite confident that it will be done.
The sort of things that happen when you work for the government are peculiar to say the least. For instance, this brief contains a section which deals with the widows of R.C.M.P. veterans. If I may read from it, it says:
-permission is granted for the payment of a gratuity to the widow of a member who dies while serving with the force, said gratuity to be equal to two months pay, provided that the deceased member had two years' service in the R.C.M. Police or has that length of service to his credit for pension purposes under the R.C.M. Police Act-
Now, listen to this:
-and was married in accordance with the R.C.M. Police rules and regulations.
I do not know whether or not they are different from those for ordinary marriages, but this is one of the conditions. If a retired member of the force dies, the widow has an immediate stoppage of pension. For example, if the ex-member died on the 7th day of the month his widow would be required to refund the balance or 23 days pension payment previously received. Now, I contend that we have to watch and be strict guardians of the public money, but I do not think that the public asks us to guard their money that strictly. As I said, according to the present rates of pay the pensions are not too bad, but it is the position of the members who retired in the early days that is causing distress, and these men are getting older all the time.
I would hate to think that ex-civil servants or ex-members of the R.C.M.P. who between now and the time legislation will be brought in, may be suffering want and hardship because this matter has been delayed from year to year.
There is nothing political in this matter. It is simply a question of what is the fair thing to do, that is fair to the ex-members of the finest police force in the world and to the ex-members of an honest and honourable civil service, a civil service which has given this country wonderful service as minister after minister has testified. I am not talking about the top bracket civil servants.
I am thinking of the chap who brings your mail and others all the way through. They are all fine people.
I have more sympathy for the man on the low income who has retired. I cannot find myself crying over the fact that a deputy minister's pension is not $2,000 more. I am thinking of these people who were mentioned by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, those on $20, $50 and $75. Those are the people that I think we should 96698-1561
Public Service-Pensions look after. We should give justice to the other people too but these people really need it and are entitled to it.
I would therefore say that this is not a political matter. It is simply a matter of how best to do it so that it is not a patchwork job, so that it is done with the interests of the recipients at heart, with due care for the financial costs as well and with the implementation of the way that the pension can be managed. I do not see anything that presents too great difficulty. I believe it can be done. I think it must be done carefully, but I think that it cannot be delayed. I think that work must be started on it as soon as possible. I hope that in the next session the government will be bringing forward legislation along the line indicated in this most admirable resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with those who have expressed their admiration for the persistence which is reflected in the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) in bringing forward year by year this resolution and at the same time to join with those who feel that in this wording the resolution probably was not wide enough and might have included, for example, employees of the C.N.R., another government agency. At the same time I am sure he must have experienced the same frustration that members on this side of the house have felt when they were sitting to the Speaker's left when they found that they could not nudge the past administration into doing something about this rather desperate situation that has been described to the house today with regard to our civil service and the R.C.M.P.
This is one occasion-and probably they will be rare in this house-when I find myself disposed to agree with my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who admires my constituency of Winnipeg South so much that he resides in it and is one of my constituents, so I understand. I would not suggest for a moment that he was disposed to vote for me. However, I have admired his demeanour in the house and his apparently inexhaustible knowledge of the rules which has been displayed to the extent of thousands of lines in Hansard in the last few days.
It is alarming to realize that as early as 1947 he started his inquiries on behalf of the civil service and was given the typical answer from the treasury bench to the effect that the matter was under consideration, and here we are 20 years later still looking at the same problem. The implication, of course, is that we on this side of the house, so many

Public Service*-Pensions of us here for the first time, should endeavour to the best of our ability to see that this matter is remedied without too much further delay. I think we can be grateful to the hon. member for Fort William, particularly those of us who are sitting on the back benches and who are freshmen-indeed, one hon. member made his baptismal speech in this house this evening on this problem and did it extraordinarily well-for bringing to our attention at an early stage the desperate need of part of our R.C.M.P. and civil service.
I was interested in the brief which was submitted by the civil service association of Ottawa who, in a canvass of some of these civil servants, more particularly perhaps those 393 with a shocking pension of less than $20 a month, received letters by way of reply with such remarks as the following:
Forced to give up long term accommodation in apartment block when rent went from $30 to $83 a month.
Had to give up my apartment for two rooms in private home.
We have bought virtually no clothing since retirement and buy lower quality food.
By dint of frugal living and careful handling of our affairs, we manage to get by.
I cut on clothing and recreation, not food, which I consider necessary for my health.
When you get replies of that kind to a canvass of ex-government employees, it is apparent that there must be many of them who are caught between the ages of 65 and 70, with perhaps a homestead which provides them with sufficient assets to remove their eligibility for a pension between the ages of 65 and 70 by way of a means test, and so for those five years they are in a position where they must live on these very frugal pensions and look forward eagerly, I am sure, to the day when they reach the age of 70 and can become eligible to receive the old age pension.
If we look at the situation as it has developed over the past 20 years we can cite, for example, the fact that prices have doubled. The consumer price index has gone from 63.2 to 123.3. The price levels in 1957 are two-thirds higher than they were in 1945 and 25 per cent higher than they were in 1949. One hundred dollars in 1939 was worth $84.78 in 1945, $57.78 in 1950 and $52.12 in 1957. Those pensioners, that large group of over 4,000 receiving less than $50 a month, are actually receiving only something in the neighbourhood of $25 or $26 a month, which would make living almost impossible without supplementary income by way of savings or by way of individual initiative in developing income of their own by taking in roomers if they still have their homesteads or taking in nursing patients if they are eligible to do so

under the bylaws of the municipality in which they live; and many of them do this.
At the same time many of them are not qualified by the nature of the employment they had in the civil service, and it is in the group of older people who had lower civil service incomes that I am sure there is the majority of the distress. If we take, for example, a clerk grade 3 we find that he would receive in 1939 a pension of $1,134. In 1945, that pension would be worth $955; in 1950 the same pension would be worth $696 per annum, and in 1957 a mere $581. How can this be regarded as a satisfactory annual pension after the recipient has put in long years of service to the government? It is quite obvious it would be impossible for any person to get by on such an amount, quite apart from the case of two persons who are married.
Only two provinces in Canada have done something to provide supplementary pensions for their employees, and those are the provinces of Saskatchewan and Newfoundland. However, even private enterprise has recognized the desperate need of some of its pensioners, and several large companies have reviewed their entire pension plan in recent years and made provision for awarding an across the board increase to those pensioners who had been longest on pension, yet who have given many years of loyal and faithful service to their companies, service which is being properly recognized by the award of an increase.
According to the brief submitted by the Ottawa civil service association, two steps may be taken. The first is to bring pensions into line with the cost of living, which they estimate would cost $3 million, and the second is to tie future increases to the increases in salaries of civil servants presently in the employ of the federal government. The association estimates that for every one per cent increase in the salaries of civil servants it would cost an additional $230,000 per year.
Now the other suggestion which is of interest to me because it would not disturb the existing legislation was the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that as an interim measure retired civil servants who are receiving very low pensions should be provided with a supplementary amount of money to bring them up to an absolute across the board basic minimum, as a fixed amount. If this were done by way of a supplementary estimate these retired civil servants would be provided with a measure of relief almost immediately which they would not otherwise receive if we went too deeply into the legislation itself and perhaps committed ourselves to a long period during which the matter would be

under consideration, such as was the experience of the opposition over the period 19471957, those deliberations being, in the end, without success. Despite this, the brief of the civil service association of Ottawa does suggest that the actuarial balance of the fund might be maintained and I quote:
In assessing the impact of such additional payments on the superannuation fund, it should be noted that $20.4 million was paid out in pensions in the fiscal year 1955-56. The proposed increase would therefore amount to about 15 per cent of present pension payments. Revenues of the fund amounted to $96 million in 1955-56, including $32.1 million in employee contributions, $32.5 million in employer contributions, and $30.9 million in interest. As a result, the year's surplus on operations of $70.7 million increased the superannuation fund to $804 million as of 1 April, 1956.
Then on page three, at appendix (b), they said, and I quote again:
If the CSAO's first recommendation were implemented, it is estimated that the second recommendation would cost $230,000 a year for a one per cent general salary increase as far as those now on pension are concerned. The capitalized value of the sums involved for those now on pension might be about $2.3 million for a one per cent salary increase. An additional $1.8 million might be required to safeguard the real value of the pensions of those civil servants retiring within the next ten years.
In view of the $70 million surplus on the superannuation fund's annual operations, as mentioned above, it would appear that the CSAO's first proposal, involving an additional $3 million, could well be implemented without increasing the 6 per cent contribution rate now in force. It would also appear that the second proposal-to safeguard future pension values-could be implemented without raising the contribution rates as long as the ratio of pensioners to employees, currently at about 1 to 11, does not drop below 1 to 6-a situation difficult to envisage.
The reason I put these quotations on record is because an actuarial analysis has apparently been made by the civil service, and from the contents of the brief it would appear that what they are seeking can be implemented without upsetting the actuarial balance of the present fund. It seems most unlikely to me that the ratio of pensioners to employees, one to eleven, at present, would ever drop below one to six. We know this is likely to be so because the number of civil servants required by the state is increasing every day. It is bound to increase with the increase in the population of our country, with the national defence situation as acute as it is at the present time, and with the increase in our social security measures. As an alternative to the suggestion of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I would recommend that the suggestion of the civil service association of Ottawa be seriously examined.
We should never forget when discussing pension problems that we have the large numbers of people across the country who
Public Service-Pensions have been self-employed on moderate incomes all their working lives. Perhaps they have operated as the sole proprietors of small businesses and raised and educated families. In their twilight years they have looked into their bank accounts and safety deposit boxes to find that while they have been great contributors to the welfare of the nation over the years and indeed have provided employment for perhaps two or three other people they have not got on hand the assets to tap which in their youth they hoped to have when the sun began to set on their period of productivity. This is due in part to inflation and sometimes to medical or hospital expenses or a number of other things.
When I think of people in this position I think of fishermen, farmers and professional people. I cannot resist placing on record the admiration I have for the individuality, initiative and forward for Canada spirit they have displayed over the years and I sympathize with them. In some vocations such as fishing and farming it may not be possible at age 60 to do what can be done by those of comparable age in office jobs. Some of these people may have had to sell their farms or fishing boats and perhaps look to spending their declining years in a small cottage in the city and feeling self-satisfied that they have perhaps put aside a nest egg of $10,000. In this day and age regardless of how well it is invested a nest egg of this amount can never return sufficient supplementary income without encroaching on capital to provide them with an adequate living particularly between ages 65 and 70. Because they have put aside that nest egg by dint of hard work they will not be eligible for pension between 65 and 70 and in all likelihood before reaching age 70 will have exhausted these moneys and in many instances have to resort to a pension on the means tests which is something extremely disturbing to a man who has stood on his own feet throughout his lifetime.
When thinking of such people you can in your mind's eye travel into Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and British Columbia to visualize the fisherman and you can in your mind's eye travel across the country to visualize the farmers and readily sympathize with their position and remember the fact that there is no government insurance plan providing for their later years; and while you can forward and support this resolution, as I do, I think it is essential that we keep these other people in mind at the same time.

Mr. Speaker, I enter this debate late in the day to make one

Public Service-Pensions or two observations and also to point out what must be apparent now to the reverend and hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). The crowning irony of his parliamentary career is that one of the things held dearest to him should have found more support among people whom he has opposed during his political career than it has apparently found among his ostensible friends.
I listened this afternoon to various members refer to the record of previous administrations in respect of the efficacy of increased pensions and superannuation payments to federal civil servants and other employees of the federal government. I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) will recall the answer he received on a previous occasion when discussing this subject and if not I will refresh his memory by referring him to page 469 of Hansard of February 17, 1947, ten years and ten months ago today-

-on which occasion in response to the hon. member's question as to whether consideration had been given by the government to increasing the pensions of superannuated federal civil servants by the addition of a cost of living bonus or other supplement the then parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance said that the question was still receiving consideration and the government's policy would be announced in due course. I refer to the quotation this evening only to point out again to the hon. member for Fort William and to others in this house that this parliamentary assistant to the minister of finance ten years ago apparently had a somewhat different attitude toward this question than has the parliamentary assistant to the present Miniser of Finance who spoke this afternoon.
There have been many debates over the years on this problem. We on this side of the house and particularly the junior members feel that the former administration deliberately stalled on this question of increased payments to superannuated and pensioned federal civil servants. We believe this because we believe that when the gentleman who was the leader of the Liberal party at the time of the question to which I referred came into this house he set the example in Canada of someone seeking a political career from a place in the civil service. We notice that this habit has been followed in that party since that time and is likely to be followed again. Sir Wilfrid Laurier could hardly have guessed the consequences of appointing to the civil service a partisan at once so able and

so ambitious who built up a personal power complex based on his affiliations in the civil service.
Mr. Speaker, I am one of the young and new members of the House of Commons who feel that we have a special moral responsibility to federal government employees. With all due respect to some of my colleagues who have expressed other opinions on the subject -we are all entitled to our private opinions as backbenchers in this party-I feel that we cannot exercise a strong position of moral suasion in respect of other pensions for other workers in Canada and we cannot advocate a greater justice for them if we deny by incaution or inactivity a greater justice for federal government employees.
What are the facts concerning retired federal civil servants? On February 13, 1957, just prior to the last debate in this house on this question which took place on March 4, the then minister of finance was asked what was the highest monthly pension paid by the government of Canada to which he replied $875. That was the highest pension paid on that date.
He was asked how many were receiving pensions of $1,000 a month or over. He replied, none. He was asked how many were receiving pensions between $500 and $999, and he replied, 28. He was asked how many were receiving pensions between $100 and $499 a month and he said, 7,067. He was asked how many were receiving pensions of between $40 and $99 a month and he said, 8,618. He was asked how many were receiving pensions of less than $40 a month and he said, 5,644.
When you look at the averages the case is even worse. The average of the 7,067 former federal civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Policemen receiving pensions of between $100 and $499 a month on February 13 last was not $499; it was $165.59. The average for the group receiving between $40 and $99 a month-that is the average for the 8,618 retired federal civil servants and retired R.C.M.P. receiving gross annual pensions of $480 to $1,088 a year-was only $67.61 a month. The average for the 5,644 getting less than $40 a month was $21.03 a month.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who has been a long-time advocate of this resolution and who must now, I think, look forward with more expectation than he has in the past for some remedial action, took part in the debate on March 4, 1957, when this matter was last discussed. At that time he alluded to a table which appeared in Hansard on February 1, 1956, which I should like to read lest anyone think

this is a political matter. Indeed, we on this side of the house feel that it may have been delayed in action because it was not notoriously a politically successful advocacy.
Eighteen months ago there were 79 retired civil servants in Newfoundland and 26 widows. In my province of Nova Scotia there	were 487 retired	civil	servants	and241 widows. In Prince Edward Island there were 64 retired civil servants and 37 widows. In New Brunswick there were 307 retired civil servants and 199 widows. In Quebec there were 2,264 retired civil servants and 1,326 widows. In Ontario there were 5,830 retired civil servants and 3,030 widows. In Manitoba there were 616 retired civil servants and 275 widows. In Saskatchewan there were	324 retired civil	servants and	121widows. In Alberta there were 531 retired civil servants and 240 widows. In British Columbia there were 2,159 retired civil servants and 757 widows, and residing elsewhere than in those 10 stated provinces there	were 341 retired	civil	servants	and206 widows. Therefore,	the	total of	the
population receiving superannuation payments in respect of federal government service is approximately 13,000 civil servants and 6,000 widows, spread almost evenly across the country in relation to population.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, we must recall in this matter some factors which I have not heard mentioned so far during the debate today. As I remarked earlier, I believe we have a moral responsibility as legislators in a federal parliament to attend to the need of federal government employees before attempting to convince or persuade other persons that they should do better than we are. We must also remember, Mr. Speaker, that federal civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Police did not have in years gone by and do not have today the same bargaining rights as other industrial and manufacturing employees. We must also recall that unless there is some assurance of some reasonable equation between purchasing powers in one year and purchasing powers in subsequent years, unless there is some reasonable assurance of some equity in purchasing powers, then all time contracts are going to be substantially meaningless and if we contract with a civil servant to pay him a superannuation based, for instance, upon a customs collector in 1937 receiving $2,620 a year from the civil service -now his salary is $5,200-if he retired at a wage of $2,620 averaged over a period immediately prior to his retirement, then his superannuation is certainly not going to be sufficient to keep him in the manner in
Public Service-Pensions which he expected it would when he retired on superannuation which he thought sufficient.
We do not think that this issue of pensions for retired civil servants and Royal Canadian Mounted Policemen can be or should be divorced from the whole area of the public service. What is it that the majority of us on this side of the house wish?

We on the back benches of this party seek a civil service neither of rulers nor of party retainers. If we do not treat retired civil servants adequately it will affect the whole morale of the active public service. We seek a public service of educated, enlightened and above all disinterested advisers, not only disinterested from the Liberal party but disinterested from our party. We want them to be able to bring to bear upon the consideration of public questions the thought and the energy of cultivated men and women, free entirely of partisan zeal not only for our opponents but for us, and undisturbed by personal or political ambition. Mr. Speaker, we are specifically dealing this evening with the victims of inflation who come directly under government control. I think we should also cast our eyes to wider and further horizons and should consider the matter of inflation as it affects other employees as well. Before I get into a couple of specific remedies which I would like to put to the house for its consideration, may I seize this opportunity, sir, of complimenting you and your deputies upon your election to preside over the affairs of this house. In the brief time this parliament has been in session, you have shown by your fairness, your courtesy and by that wonderful sense of humour, what a proper officer of parliament should be. I feel, sir, that you have kept the house reasonably free from the excesses of the maidens now sitting in opposition and who used to sit on the treasury benches and also, to be fair, from the excesses of the maidens who now sit on the treasury benches and who used to be in opposition.
I am sorry I was not in the house this afternoon to hear the beginning of this debate. We on the external affairs committee are keeping hours that are almost rivalling those maintained by this house. It seems to me the remedy that we consider should be considered in the light of the fact that government has two aspects. The first aspect of government to keep in mind in a debate like this is that the government is an employer, either itself or through the medium of crown corporations. The second aspect of government to bear in mind is the broader sense of the conduct of the affairs of the nation that touch on the lives of all Canadians. Now, could we solve the one problem, the lowered purchasing power of the civil servants and the retired mounted police officers, I ask, without being unfair to the others? Since I was not here, I do not know if any information was presented as to what industry has done to solve the problem for those who retired on pension during the years 1930 to 1940.
However, I believe we do have an immediate remedy at hand for those under our direct control, that is the civil servants and R.C.M.P. who have retired. I believe that was set forth this afternoon in the remarks, which unfortunately I did not hear, of the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). Now, sir, inflation points out the need for some remedy which can adjust itself to the disease. The remedy needed is one which has, at least, the factor of growth. This evening we were told by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Chown) that the dollar today is worth
Public Service-Pensions about 50 per cent of what it was 18 years ago. I draw a parallel between the loss of purchasing power of these pensions and the losses in other fields as a result of inflation. I think, for example, of insurance investment. The life insurance dollar has certainly not done the job we would like it to do and that is because inflation has knocked down its value. If $10 were invested in 1946, and that was the first touch the insurance agent made upon me, it is probably worth about $6 or $7 today.
The difficulty, as I see it, with pensions and with insurance investments is that those are the orthodox type of investments and subject to very strict dominion and provincial laws. These investments are restricted pretty well on the security side, that is things like bonds and mortgages, rather than the equity side, that is the ownership of shares. Shares, as we know, can adjust themselves as capital appreciates in value, and the shares will go up in value too. I should like to make this suggestion, if I may, so we can come to grips perhaps with the larger problem that confronts us, not only the one so ably put forward by the hon. members for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), but the problem of the people outside who are not retired civil servants or R.C.M.P. Perhaps we should relax the present laws so that pensions may be related to appreciation or growth, or call it inflation if you will.
Another possible remedy, which might sound rather radical, and certainly one that would have to be given a great deal of consideration-I think of it offhand, and I am not particularly wedded to the idea-is a tie-in somewhere of rents to the matter of pensions. Rents will go up in good times. They are certainly a more correct barometer or index to financial growth, as anyone who has had his rent raised will appreciate, than the more orthodox type of investment to which pensions are now anchored. The solution may be to turn the pension fund into some form of housing development on the equity side. I thank the house for its consideration.
