I should like to assure the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), who has sponsored this resolution, that I have always been heartily in favour of the sentiment contained therein.
I rise tonight, Mr. Speaker, because as I listened to the discussion, and I followed most of it today, I felt that for the first time it would appear that we are going to get somewhere in regard to the implementation of this resolution. I thought the contribution of the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Bell) was especially forthright and left no uncertainty at all concerning the attitude of the present administration to this difficult problem. I quite appreciate that it is a complex problem. He outlined the consideration that had been given already and indicated that rather than any delaying action the minister, the parliamentary assistant and the officials of the finance department are giving it the most urgent and anxious consideration possible.
The hon. member for Fort William and myself have often been allied in worthwhile causes of this kind and this was another reason for my desire to say a few words at this time, to vocally express my admiration for his contributions to the many topics discussed in this house during the long years he has sat here, and also to indicate my personal support for this particular recommendation.
This resolution refers only to two categories affected by the general problem of pensioners at this time. He refers to the civil servants and to the members of the R.C.M.P. I want to take this opportunity to mention another category of pensioner that is most severely affected by the inflationary trends of recent years. It is a group who come under the old militia pension act. It is not a large category. As a matter of fact, my special interest in this resolution arises from just a few cases of the kind that exist in my constituency.
I have had one or two former members of the permanent force retired under the old militia pension act who have been contacting me regularly with reference to this difficulty. I have made certain representations in writing


to the minister of finance in years gone by. No action was taken because of the general tendency to postpone action on this problem. However, I am presenting this special aspect of the difficulty tonight, hoping that the comprehensive considerations that were outlined by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance will be broad enough to extend to this category as well as the others. These people, while not so numerous as the civil servants generally or even the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are suffering under the same financial disability.
In reference to a problem of this kind there immediately arises the question as to where the necessary financial resources are coming from in order to implement this recommendation. The hon. member for Fort William, in his usual forthright manner presented the thought that perhaps a special tax on tobacco and liquor might solve the difficulty. It is true that those two particular commodities yield a substantial percentage of our tax returns. As a matter of fact, I remember that a former minister of finance-I refer to Hon. Douglas Abbott-who was a nonsmoker himself when questioned on this point or whenever he was offered a cigarette, his invariable reply was, "I don't smoke 'em; I just tax 'em". It is true that tobacco as well as liquor has yielded a high rate of tax return.
I cannot agree with the hon. member for Fort William that funds sufficient to meet the increased public expenditure required for bringing up the depressed position of civil servants and mounted police and the other categories into line with the prevailing cost of living could be derived from this one source. But after listening to the parliamentary assistant this afternoon, I am quite sure that he and his associates are dealing with the broader aspects in this regard and that they will be able to come up with a suitable solution.
I do not want to prolong this discussion unduly tonight, Mr. Speaker.

As I have indicated, I have never had an opportunity previously to speak on this matter. There is only one further point that I should like to make at this time. The point has been made tonight that the unfortunate circumstances in which our retired civil servants find themselves are the result of inflationary trends. I feel that statement is only partially true. We have been beset with what is called creeping inflation where prices and wages, at least in the last 20 years, have been rising continuously whereas those on fixed incomes feel themselves to be remaining at the stationary level. In other

I know it is not put there in a formal way but the trend has been for labour and management, in terms of wages and prices, to be on a very exhilarating escalator ride whereas those on fixed incomes, such as those whom we are discussing tonight, find themselves in a static and relatively depressed position.
